OBITUARY REFERENCE  
MR. CHAIRMAN: Hon. Members, I refer with profound sorrow, to the passing away of Dr. 
(Kumari) Sarojini Babar, a former Member of this House on the 20th April, 2008 at the age of 
89 years.  
Born at Bagni in the Sangli district of Maharashtra in January, 1920, Dr. Babar had her 
education at the University of Pune, Tilak Vidyapith, Pune and Sahityani Sanskriti Mandal 
Mumbai.  
A litterateur, Dr. Babar was associated with various educational and cultural institutions. Dr. 
Babar served as Chairman of the Maharashtra State Folklore Committee, Maharashtra Sahitya 
Parishad and Maharashtra Lok Sahitya Parishad. Dr. Babar had many publications to her credit. 
She was also Editor of the 'Samaj Shikshan Mala', published from Pune.  
The legislative career of Dr. Babar commenced with the membership of the Maharashtra 
legislative Assembly, where she was a Member from 1 952 to 1957. She also served as a 
Member of the Maharashtra Legislative Council from 1963 to 1966. Dr. Babar represented the 
State of Maharashtra in this House from April, 1968 to April, 1974.  
In the passing away of Dr. Sarojini Babar, the country has lost a distinguished litterateur and an 
able Parliamentarian.  
I request hon. Members to rise in their places and observe silence as a mark of respect to the 
memory of the departed.  
(Hon. Members then stood in silence for one minute) 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Secretary-General will convey to the members of the bereaved family our 
deep sense of sorrow and sympathy.  
ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS  
Meeting shortage of Officers in the Army  
*421.   SHRIMATI SYEDA ANWARA TAIMUR: tt 
SHRI VIJAYAJ. DARDA:  
Will the Minister of DEFENCE be pleased to state:  
(a) whether Short-Service Commissioned Officers and Officers from Territorial Units, after usual 
NDA pattern training, can significantly contribute towards meeting the shortage of over 11,000 
officers in the Army; and  
†† The question was actually asked on the floor of the House by Shrimati Syeda Anwara Taimur . 

2    Oral  Answers  [RAJYA SABHA]  to Questions  
(b) if so, whether an indepth study will be undertaken through internationally or nationally 
renowned Defence experts in this regard so that maximum number of our boys from schools/ 
colleges are motivated towards joining the Defence Forces?  
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF DEFENCE (SHRI M.M. PALLAM 
RAJU): (a) and (b) A Statement is laid on the Table  of the House.  
Statement  
(a) and (b) Short Service Commissioned Officers (SSC) are an integral part of the Defence 
Forces. The SSC Officers are trained on similar pattern as imparted by the National Defence 
Academy (NDA), except that it is for a shorter duration and at a different Academy. However, 
the Territorial Army is set up to augment and relieve the regular army of their static duties 
during national emergencies and for providing aid t o the civil authorities in dealing with 
natural calamities and maintenance of essential services.  
The shortage of officers in the Defence Forces is both in the Permanent Commission as 
well as in the various SSC Cadres. There is a provision for grant of Permanent Commission to 
willing SSC (Men) officers, provided they fulfill the eligibility criteria. Intake of SSC officers 
do contribute towards meeting the shortage of offic ers. However, since the existing total 
cadre strength of SSC officers itself is less, it will not be able to meet the shortage of officers 
in-any significant manner. Similarly, there is a provision for officers of the Territorial Army, 
who volunteer and meet the prescribed criteria, to be considered for grant of Short Service 
Commission. However, the number of such officers is less to make any significant contribution 
to meet the shortage of officers in the Army.  
There is no proposal by the Services to conduct any study by engaging internationally or 
nationally renowned Defence experts. However, a num ber of in-house studies have been 
conducted by the Defence Services on the issue. In addition, the Defence Forces have 
undertaken a number of sustained image projection a nd publicity campaigns to create 
awareness among the youth on the advantages of taki ng up a challenging and satisfying 
career.  
The Shortfall in recruitment of officers in the Army is largely due to change in the socio-
economic environment and the resultant changes in c areer preferences, better employment 
opportunities in other sectors, tough selection pro cedures and service conditions of the 
Defence Forces.  
A number of measures have been intiated by the Defence Forces to address the problem 
of shortage of officers which include candidate-fri endly recruitment procedures to attract 
more number of candidates and a focused publicity d rice in various institutions to attract 
potential candidates. Awareness campaigns, particip ation in career fairs and exhibitions, 
advertisements in print and electronic media, counselling and motivational talks in schools, 
colleges and NCC camps are also some of the other measures in this direction. In addition, 
the commitment and bravery of the Armed Forces is c onsistently projected through the 
electronic and print media.  
SHRIMATI SYEDA ANWARA TAIMUR: Sir, I would like to know from the hon. Minister, 
since the inception of the Short Service Commission , how many officer from all the three 
Services have been inducted into the Short Service Commission so far and how many of 
them are men and women?  

Oral Answers  [23 APRIL, 2008]  to Questions   3 
SHRI M.M. PALLAM RAJU: Sir, the total number of Short Service Commission officers in 
the Army is 3312; in the Nevy, it is 1257 and, in the Air Force 1771. As of now, rules permit only 
men to be inducted into the permanent commission.  
SHRIMATI SYEDAANWARATAIMUR: Sir, women are inducted only as Short Service 
Commission officers; all the three Services offer only Short Service Commission to women 
officers. The Short Service Commission has an initial compulsory contractual tenure of five 
to seven years, which, depending upon the service, is extendable up to a minimum term of ten 
years. This was reviewed in the year 2002 and all the three Services extended the term of the 
Short Service Commission to 14 years. Unlike other male officers who have the option of a 
permanent commission at the time of joining, women officers are not extended the option of 
a permanent commission at any stage in their service. At the end of their maximum tenure of 
14 years, they have to leave the Services. The ceil ing of their tenure in the Services has a 
serious limiting effect on the career of women officers, as they reach a certain date in their 
career while they are in their early or mid 30s.  
MR. CHAIRMAN: Question please.  
SHRIMATI SYEDAANWARATAIMUR: As long as the women officers in the Services 
are denied the choice of a permanent commission, th eir services in the armed forces will 
remain merely a job and not a dedicated career option. Now, I would like to know from the 
hon. Minister whether the Government is planning to  extend the option of permanent 
commission to the women officers with the male officers. If not, why? Why is this disparity 
and discrimination when women are employed on equit able terms, and will there be any 
meaning in placing further opportunities for men?  
SHRI M.M. PALLAM RAJU: Sir, the Ministry is totally empathetic to the situation. As of 
now, like as I said earlier, the rules only permit men to be inducted into the permanent 
commission. There was a Committee formed, consisting of the Chiefs of Staff which looked 
into the matter, and has given certain recommendations. If you would recall, Sir, in the last 
Session, the hon. Raksha Mantri also said that we a re looking into the matter of inducting 
women into the permanent commission, and the Raksha Mantri has been consistently following 
the matter in the Ministry.

SHR1 M.M. PALLAM RAJU: Mr. Chairman, Sir, this is a matter of concern, but it is not a 
matter of alarm. We know there is a shortage of officers and a lot of officers are also trying to 
leave because of the incredible opportunities that are arising in the private sector. I can say 
that pay is not necessarily the only factor that attracts men and women to the armed forces. 
As you are' aware, Sir, the conditions of services and the terms of employment in the armed 
services are challenging, and we are constantly see king to improve that to make it more 
attractive for the officers' cadre. Similarly, we are also trying to improve the overall situation 
for everybody. But, at this stage, the shortage and  the people who are trying to leave is 
primarily from the non-select ranks which are the officers who are actually leading the men on 
the ground. The Ministry is doing its best to improve the service conditions, and, again, the 
Raksha Mantri has taken up the matter after the Sixty Pay Commission recommendations to 
see how well we can compensate our officers better.

SHRIMATIJAYA BACHCHAN: Sir, there is scarcity offic ers and there are a number of 
vacancies which are to be filled up. Has the Govern ment evolved any emergency or 
extraordinary plan to fill up these vacancies? If n ot, why? What are you doing with the 
amount that is accumulated which you have not been able to pay as salary due to these 
vacancies?  
SHRI M.M. PALLAM RAJU: Sir, the Ministry is doing a ll that it can to address the 
shortage of officers in the non-select ranks, like improving the service conditions and 
increasing the number of intake channels especially the Short-Service Commission channel 
and the Technical Entry Scheme channel. These are also the measures, which we are taking 
to increase the capacities in the two premier insti tutions that we have, that is, the NDA and 
the Indian Military Academy at Dehradun, and also the OTA. Regarding the pay, I think, after 
the Sixty Pay Commisison recommendations again thes e matters are being pressed for re-
examination especially for the non-select rank offivers' pay scales and the pay scales of the * 
soldiers on the ground.

MR. CHAIRMAN: You can raise that point.

Loss of jobs in SSI Units due to appreciation in Rupee value  
t*422. SHRI RAJ MOHINDER SINGH MAJITHA:tt DR. 
MURLIMANOHAR JOSHI:  
Will the Minister of LABOUR AND EMPLOYMENT be pleased to state:  
(a) whether it is a fact that due to appreciation in value of Indian Rupee against dollar and 
4 lakh units being closed in small industry sector, 13 lakh workers are likely to be rendered 
jobless during 2007; and  
(b) if not, the assessment of Government thereto?  
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF LABOURAND EMPLOYMENT (SHRI 
OSCAR ]FERNANDES): (a) and (b) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House.  
Statement  
(a) and (b) The rupee appreciated by 9.8 per cent a gainst the US dollar during the last 
financial year between April 3,2007, and January 16,2008. The impact of rupee appreciation has 
been acutely felt by the exporting community, in particular, by those sectors which are labour 
intensive, whose inputs are less import driven, and  where value addition is low. Loss of 
employment, output and consequently steep reduction in exports against the target set has 
become a reality. In order to assess the impact of the rupee appreciation, a Committee was set 
up under the Ministry of Commerce and Industry.  
The question was actually asked on the floor of the  House by Shri Raj Mohinder Singh 
Majitha  
Details of the findings of the Committee are given below in Statement I & II.

SHRI JAIRAM RAMESH: Sir, as is well known, the policy of the Government of India and of 
the successive Governments has been to give priority to multilateral trade negotiations. Our 
effort has always been to have a multilateral trade agreement under the aegis of the WTO. 
However, pending the conclusion of the Doha Round, many countries have gone into bilateral Free 
Trade Agreements. India cannot afford to remain a mute spectator to this. That is why, India too 
has started negotiating FTAs with a number of countries. The hon. Member wants to know with 
how many countries, we have FTAs as of now. As of now, Sir, we have five Free Trade Agreements. 
We have a Free Trade Agreement with Sri Lanka. We have a South Asian Free Trade Agreement, 
which is, SAFTA. We have a Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement with Singapore. We 
have a Free Trade

Agreements.

SHRI JAIRAM RAMESH: Sir, as far as Bahgladesh is co ncerned, our total exports to 
Bangaldesh are close to $ 2 billions. Our imports from Bangladesh are about $ 200 billion. 
In fact, we have a huge trade surplus with Banglade sh, not a trade deficit. Now, as far as 
linking our trade with transit is coneficerned, we have always been requesting the 
Bangladesh Government to look at the issue of trans it rights through Bangladesh 
seriously. We have not been very successful. But, w e have not held back increasing trade 
as far as Bangladesh is concerned. As far as Pakistan is concerned, the hon. Member is well 
aware that Pakistan does not grant us the Most Favoured Nation status. In spite of the fact 
that Pakistan has not given India an MFN status, wh ich we have given to Pakistan since 
mid 90's, we have increased our trade with Pakistan . Our exports to Pakistan are about $ 
1.6 billion and our imports for Pakistan are about $ 400 million. So, we have a huge trade 
surplus with Pakistan. As far as China is concerned , we do not have a Free Trade 
Agreement. We have a Joint Study Group which is examining the feasibility of having a Free 
Trade Agreement. However, trade between India and C hina has increased spectacularly. 
Imports from China have gone up. Our exports to China have also gone up. I do not think 
it is possible to look at trade balances only in te rms of specific countries. We must look at 
the overall balance of payments and judge from that point of view. I do not think our trade 
with China is cause for any alarm.  
SHRI B.J. PANDA: Sir, of all these Trade Agreements , the most important one is the 
SAFTA which concerns our immediate neighbours. Rece ntly, the hon. Minister's senior 
Cabinet colleague was quoted in the media that our MFN status to Pakistan is now under 
review or would be reviewed because they are not re ciprocating the same facilities to us. 
Would the hon. Minister tell us if Pakistan is, in fact, required to give us MFN status under 
the SAFTAAgreement? Is it at all our interest to cancel our MFN status to them, because we 
have a lot of third country exports to them, which go through Dubai and other countries? Is 
it at all in our interest to consider reviewing this, or, are they required to give it to us?  
SHRI JAIRAM RAMESH: Sir, the grant of MFN status is under the WTO regime. Granting 
MFN status means the country will not discriminate against others. It is a fundamental 
principle of international trade. America does not give MFN status to Cuba and Pakistan 
does not give MFN status to India. These are the two examples where the MFN principle has, 
indeed, been violated. However, Sir, the policy of the successive Governments has been that 
even though Pakistan has not given us the MFN statu s, we should continue to pursue 
economic engagements with Pakistan. That policy has been a success. As I mentioned, our 
exports to Pakistan today, our legal exports to Pakistan, direct exports to Pakistan is about

violation of international law but we do not want to hold that up to pursue economic ties with 
Pakistan.

SHRIJ AI RAM RAMESH: Sir, I have already answered this question in a previous Session of this 
House that while there is indeed a Joint Study Group to examine the feasibility of a Free Trade 
Agreement between India and China, this is an issue in which there are deep divisions, both 
within the Government as well as within Indian indsutry. No final decision will be taken on a Free 
Trade Agreement with China without consultation with all stakeholders including industry. As of 
now, Sir, pursuing of a Free Trade Agreement with C hina is not a priority as far as the 
Government is concerned.  
SHRI N.K. SINGH: Sir, I would like to find out from the hon. Minister that in terms of the 
total number of FTAs which the hon. Minister has enumerated we are undertaking, whether 
any study has been made on studying the efficacy an d value of Free Trade Agreements 
versus a multilateral trading system and to what ex tent Free Trade Agreement are trade 
deflection instead of being incremental in enhancing the multiplier gains from trade.  
' SHRI JAIRAM RAMESH: Sir, there is no question absolutely in my mind as in the mind of 
most Economists and trade experts that Free Trade Agreements are the second best option. It 
is not the best option. The best option remains mul tilateral trade negotiations rule-based 
under the aegis of the WTO. However, as I explained , because of the continued impasse, 
particularly, on Doha round, many countries and blocks of countries have restorted to having 
bilateral Free Trade Agreements. And, Sir, India wi ll get edged out of regional and 
international markets if it too does not pursue thi s course. However, I share the hon. 
Member's concern that this is not an optimal route.  We should continue to pursue multi-
lateral trade liberalisation even as we pursue selectively Free Trade Agreements.  
As far as the study is concerned, Sir, this matter is under review constantly. The Indo-Sri 
Lanka Free Trade Agreement has been the longest in existence, and I can categorically say 
that the Indo-Sri Lanka Free Trade Agreement is an outstanding example of success both 
for India we well as Sri Lanka. In fact,, the polit ical and strategic relationship between the 
two countries has been transformed because of the success of the FTA. The other FTA that 
has been in existence for quite some time is the on e with Singapore and even with 
Singapore our trade balance is broadly good. Our ex ports to Singapore are about six-and-a 
half billion dollars and our imports are also about six-and-a-half billion dollars.  
So, I want to assure the hon. Member that the impact of the FTAs are constantly under study 
and if we find that the FTAs are working against our interests, we will take preventive measures to 
protect Indian industry and Indian agriculture.

*425. SHRI SU. THIRUNAVUKKARASAR: Will the Minister of RURAL DEVELOPMENT 
be pleased to state:  
(a)  how many kilometres distance was constructed under the Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak 
Yojana (PMGSY) in 2007-08; 
(b)  how many villages are yet to be connected with the main roads; and 
(c)  the total number of roads and kilometres requested by all State Government, State-
wise under the scheme?

(a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the table of the House.  
(a)  Under Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana (PMGSY), during the year 2007-08 (upto 
February 2008) 30799.30 km roads have been construc ted and/or upgraded. This includes 
new connectivity length of 22417.19 km and upgraded length of 8362.11 km.

is the habitation. As per the latest data available, 166938 number of habitations are eligible to  
be connected under PMGSY out of which 45506 habitat ions have been connected under 
PMGSY out of whch 45506 habitations have been connected. In addition, 18142 habitations 
have been reported as connected by the States under other schemes. The State-wise details 
regarding number of habitations eligible under PMGSY and length of road to be constructed 
have been given in the enclosed Statement.

Extreme change in weather patterns  
*428. SHR1MATIJAYABACHCHAN: Will the Minister of EARTH SCIENCES be pleased 
to state:  
(a)  whether India Meteorological Department has studied the extreme changes reflected 
in the weather patterns in the northern and other parts of the country this year; 
(b)  whether any observations have been made on the causes of extreme wheather or the 
trends to come; and 
(c)  if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF EARTH SCIENCES (SHRI KAPIL SIBAL): (a) to (c) India 
Meteorological Department (IMD) has been studying the trends of the important wheather 
parameters and also constantly monitoring the occurrence of extreme wheather events over 
various parts of the country. Data pertaining to the period 1901—2005 suggests that annual 
mean temperature for the country as a whole has risen to 0.51°C over the period. A study, 
which focuses on monsoon season, clearly shows that though mean monsoon rainfall 
remained stable (without any increasing or decreasing trend) over the Indian sub-continent, 
the frequency of occurrence of extreme rain events has increased about 1% per year during 
past 50 years.  
These trends may be explained in the backdrop of global warming and increasing trend in 
the mean temperature of earth over the past 50 years. Increase in air temperature increases 
the mositure holding capacity through the amplification of instability arising from small local 
disturbances. In the coming decades, increasing trends of extreme weather events are likely 
to increase for most of the parts of India. Some of the important weather events of this year 
are given in the Statement (See below).  
The excess rainfall during March, 2008 over South Peninsula was due to enhanced 
activitiy of the easterly waves over the equatorial  Indian Ocean. The sea surface 
temperature and wind anomalies over the equatorial Indian Ocean observed during 
the month were favourable for such excess rainfall activity over South peninsula. 
This kind of rainfall activity has been observed in the past also. However, the amount 
of rainfall received over South peninsula during th e month of March, 2008 was 
unprecedented.  
Determining whether a specific, single extreme event is due to a specific cause is difficult 
as (i) Extreme events are usually caused by a combination of wheather factors and (ii) A wide 
range of extreme events is a normal occurrence even  in an unchanging climate 
(Intergovernmental Pannel on Climate Change—4th Assessment Report).

3106. SHRI N.R. GOVINDARAJAR: 
SHRI KAMAL AKHTAR:

wise production of cement by all the cement manufactures in the country;

against the manufacturers found responsible therefor?

per the Cement Manufacturers' Association, the tota l production of cement was 127.57

Job losses due to entry of multi-brand retailers  
3126. SHRI RAMDAS AGARWAL: Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY 
be pleased to state:  
(a)  whether Government is aware that multi-brand retailers like US based Wal-Mart and 
France's Carrefour would drive thousands of small store people in India out of business and 
cause tens of thousands of job losses; 
(b)  whether Government is also aware of the difficulties being faced by small manufacturers 
and traders who are having 97 per cent of India's retail trade in the unorganised market; and 
(c)  if so, what steps Government have taken so far to p rotect the interests of "Kiryana" 
stores and increasing number of unemployed youth in the country? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DEPARTMENT OF INDUSTRIAL POLICY AND 
PROMOTION MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI ASHWANI KUMAR): 
(a) As per extant policy, Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) is not allowed in retail trade except 
in retail trade of Single Brand products where FDI up to 51 % is permitted with prior Government 
approval.  
(b) and (c) Government has instituted a study to assess the impact of organized retailing 
on unorganized retail trade with respect to various  aspects, including the impact on 
employment and on small traders, through Indian Cou ncil for Research on International 
Economic Relations (ICRIER). Government has also commissioned a study to the National 
Council of Applied Economic Research (NCAER) on Gro wth linkages of Foreign Direct 
Investment (FDI) in India which would focus on the impact of FDI on rural economy. The 
final reports are yet to be submitted by these organisations.

3127. SHRI B.K. HARIPRASAD: Will the Minister of DEFENCE be pleased to state:  
(a) whether the P. Rama Rao Committee has recommended through overhaul of the working 
of Defence Research & Development Organisation by restricting its activities only on high 
tech areas;

(b)  whether most of the arms equipment development proj ects including Light Combat 
Aircraft undertaken by DRDO has ended up in huge time and cost overruns; and 
(c)  whether the rate of indeginisation on DRDO developd equipments has only touched 
30 per cent against the target of 70 per cent set for the Tenth Plan? 
THE MINISTER OF DEFENCE (SHRI A.K. ANTONY): (a) The Defence Research and 
Development Organisation (DRDO) Review Committee constituted by the Government to 
suggest measure for improving the functioning of DRDO inter alia Ministry of Defence, and 
Services has submitted its report to the Government on 5th March, 2008. It is under study of 
the Government.  
(b)  There had been delays in some of the DRDO projects due to some genuine difficulties, 
like technical complexities, technological embargo/sanctions, non-availability of infrastructure 
within the country, extended and long lasting user trials, revision of systems specifications 
during development phase, etc. Besides many constra ints, DRDO had equipped services 
with state-of-the-art technologies in the field of strategic systems, battle tanks, electronic 
warfare and communication systems, armour and armam ents, life support systems, naval 
systems, missile systems, aerospace systems, etc. 
(c)  Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) is developing only defence-
critical/denied technologies and strategic systems.  In this area, DRDO has ensured 100% 
self-reliance. As far as the tactical systems are concerned, DRDO is responsible for design, 
development, trials and evaluation as and when task ed by Government. Acceptance of 
DRDO developed systems and their subsequent product ion and induction depends on 
users and identified production agencies, Defence Public Sector Undertakings (DPSUs) and 
Ordanance Factories (OFs). Achieving self-reliance is a responsibility that has to be met 
through national effort by DPSUs, OFs, Private industries and DRDO, jointly. DRDO works 
with the production agencies to resolve the major problems during the production.

Scheme for protection of witnesses  
3169. SHRI SHANTARAM LAXMAN NAIK: Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be 
pleased to state:  
(a)  whether Government proposes to enforce any scheme for the protection of witnesses; and 
(b)  if so, the details of essential features of the scheme? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRIMATI V. 
RADHIKA SELVI): (a) The Law Commission of India in its 198th Report on 'Witness Identity 
Protection and Witness Protection Programmes' has suggested comprehensive review of witness 
protection. Since, the Criminal Law and the Criminal Procedure are on the Concurrent List of the 
Seventh Schedule to the Constitution of India this requires consultation with State Governments 
and Union Territory Administrations. The Report has been referred to all the State Government and 
Union Territory Administration for their comments/views. No time frame can be fixed in this 
regard.  
(b) Witness Protection Programmes refer to witness protection outside the Court. At the 
instance of the public prosecutor, the witness can be given a new identity by a Magistrate after 
conducting an exparte inquiry in his chambers. In a case of likelihood of danger to his life, he is 
given a different identity and may, if need be, even relocated in different place along with his 
depandants till the trial of the case against the a ccused is completed. The expenses for 
maintenance of all the persons must be met by the State Legal Aid Authority through the District 
Legal Aid Authority. The witness has to sign an MoU which will list out the obligations of the State 
as well the witness. Being admitted to the programme, the witness has an obligation to depose 
and the State has an obligation to protect him physically outside Court. Breach of MoU by the 
witness will result in his being taken out of the programme.

Relief Fund (CRF) has been constituted for each State, which is contributed by Government 
of India and the State Governments in the ratio of 75:25. Central contribution is release J in 
two equal installments. Additional assistance is al so provided to the States in the wake of 
calamities of severe nature from National Calamity Contingency Fund (NCCF), as per laid 
down procedure. Government of India supplements the efforts of the State Governments by 
providing logistic and financial support.

2007-08 amounting to Rs. 70.70 croreto Kerala.

THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR AND EMPLOYMENT 
(SHRI OSCAR FERNANDES): (a) to (c) As per two most recent quinqucnnial rounds of 
National Sample Survey Organisation (NSSO) on emplo yment and unemployment, 
unemployment rate on Current Daily Status basis has  been estimated at 7.31% in 1999-

98    Written Answers to  [RAJYA SABHA]  Unstarred  Questions  
The Eleventh Five Year Plan provides a framework to  restructure policies to achieve a 
new vision based on faster, more broad-based and in clusive growth. It aims at making 
employment generation an integral part of the growt h process and devise strategies to 
accelerate not only growth of employment but also of wages of the poorly paid. The Eleventh 
Plan document approved by National Development Coun cil has proejcted that 58 million 
job opportunities on Current Daily Status are likel y to be created during the Eleventh Plan 
period. Besides, Government of India is implementin g various employment generation 
and poverty alleviation programmes in both rural an d urban areas to increase employment 
opportunities. Some of the important ones are-Swara na Jayanti Shahari Rozgar Yojana 
(SJSRY); Prime Minister's Rozgar Yojana (PMRY); Swarnjayanti Gram Swarozgar Yojana 
(SGSY); Rural Employment Generation Programme (REGP); Sampoorna Grameen Rozgar 
Yojana (SGRY) and National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (NREGA), 2005.  
Steps have been initiated to identify and implement systematic reforms in administration 
of Industrial Training Institutes (ITIs) so as to facilitate closer interaction with the industry 
in order to improve quality of training, make the graduates better employable and help them 
earn decent wages.

Policy to prevent brain drain  
†3204. SHRI JAI PARKASH AGGARWAL: Will the Minister  of LABOUR AND 
EMPLOYMENT be pleased to state:  
(a)  whether Central Government has taken or proposes to take any steps to formulate are 
appropriate and effective policy in order to preven t brain drain which is constantly taking 
place in different sectors; 
(b)  if so, the details thereof as on date; and 
(c)  if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR AND EMPLOYMENT 
(SHRI OSCAR FERNANDES): (a) to (c) in view of global nature of scientific enterprise, the 
Government is of the view that scientific mobility should not be disturbed. The scientists 
move overseas in view of better opportunities available for higher education and employment 
in the emerging area of Science and Technology. Inc reasing opportunities in India have 
attracted many scientists to return to India particularly in some of the high-tech areas like IT. 
Availability of Indian diaspora overseas has also b een of great help in undertaking joint 
research projects/ventures in the country. Government has taken a number of initiatives and 
measures in order to improve the working conditions of scientists to encourge their retention/ 
return in the country.

3205. SHRI SANJAY RAUT: Will the Minister of LABOUR AND EMPLOYMENT be 
pleased to state:

training to the rescued child labourers during the last three years; and 
(b)  the number of child labourers benefited during this period, particularly in Maharashtra

THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR AND EMPLOYMENT 
(SHRI OSCAR FERNANDES): (a) Government is implementing the National Child Labour 
Projects (NCLP) Scheme in 250 districts of 20 State s of the country. Under the Scheme, 
children working in identified hazardous occupation s and processes are withdrawn from 
work and put in Special Schools where they are prov ided with vocational training, 
accelerated bridging education, nutrition, stipend and healthcare facilities etc. In addition, 
another project, namely INDUS Child Labour Project is being implemented in collaboration 
with the US Department of Labour since 2004 in 21 D istricts of the country. Under the 
project, vocational training is also being provided  to the adolescents in the age group of

3208. SHRI ABU ASIM AZMI: Will the Minister of RURA L DEVELOPMENT be 
pleased to state:  
(a)  whether union Government is fully confident that 100 days employment programme 
has been fully implemented in the country, State-wise; 
(b)  if so, whether the labour accounts have also been o pened in the banks and the post 
offices in the villages; 
(c)  the State-wise number of such labourers who are cov ered under 100 days Rozgar 
Yojana; 
(d)'whether 100 days income is sufficient to the family of the labour for 365 days; and  
(e) how long a labour has to wait for another 100 days employment?.  
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT (SHRI 
CHANDRA SEKHAR SAHU): (a) National Rural Employment  Guarantee act, 2005 was 
launched in 200 districts in its first phase of implements on 2.2.2006. The Act was extended to 
130 additional districts in 2007-2008 and has been extended to all the remaining rural areas of 
the country with effect from 1.4.2008. the Act prov ides a legal guarantee of 100 days of 
employment to every rural household in a financial year whose adult members volunteer to

instructions have been issued to all Sates for open ing accounts of NREGA workers in Bank and Post 
Offices. So far 1,39,63,377 accounts of NREGA worke rs have been opened in Banks and Post Offices.  
 (c)~NREGS is demand based. The basic unit for provi ding employment under NREGA is a 
'household' and not an individual. Adult members of  a rural household are required to register 
themselves with the Gram Panchayat for issue of a j ob card. Job Card is issued to a households 
after verification of the details given in the appl ication. State-wise number of household who 
have been issued job cards under NREGS is given in column ,2 of the Statement mentioned at

The aim of NREGA is to provide for the enhancement of livelihood security of the rural households by 
providing at least 100 days of guaranteed wage empl oyment in every financial year to every household 
whose adult members volunteer to do unskilled manua l work. NREGA is demand based. Under 'the Act, 
employment is provided to a wage seeker for the num ber of days of employment demanded subject to 
"art over all ceiling of 100 days per household in a financial year. Members of the household may avai l 
other available employment opportunities in additio n to the 100 days of guaranteed employment per 
household provided under the Act on demand. 
(d)  100 days of Employment under NREGA can be availed o f on demand by a rural household any 
time in a financial year as per the provisions of t he Act.

Siphoning of money under NREGA  
3209. MS. MABEL REBELLO: 3VUltheMinisterofRURALDEVE LOPMENT,.be 
pleased to state:  v 
(a)  whether Government is aware that the Gram Sahayaks are taking almost 25 per cent 
of the allotted money under NREGA for sanctioning/construction of wells; 
(b)  the district, block and Panchayat officials siphone d off almost 40 per cent of cash 
of NREGA projects and in what manner Government propose to eliminate corruption from 
these projects; and   
(c)  in what manner Government proposes to rectify this situation of corruption and 
harassment of tribal beneficiaries by junior offici als !ike the BDO and his subordinates 
who execute NREGA projects? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT (SHRI 
CHANDRA SEKHAR SAHU): (a) Operational Guidelines fo r NREGA provide that one 
Gram Rozgar Sahayak (GRS) should be appointed in each Gram Panchayat. Duties of a RS 
include registration of households, issue of job ca rds, issue of dated receipt against job 
application, allocation of work, payment of wages a nd un-employment allowance, 
maintenance of records and any other duty prescribed by the State Employment Guarantee 
Council. His duties of not include sanctioning/construction of wells.  
(b) and (c) Ministry of Rural Development requested  CAG to undertake performance 
audit of the implementation of NREGA in 68 phase I districts for the year 2006-2007. Some 
irregularities have been reported in the implementation of NREGS. These irreyularities mainly 
relate to procedures such as application for employ ment, issue of dated resouipts, job card 
formals, muster rolls, maintenance of record registers. In addition, complaints', have also been 
received regarding irregularities in the implementation of NREGA. State-wise details of the  

120    Written Answers to  [RAJYA SABHA]  Unstarred  Questions  
complaints along with the action taken by the Minis try thereon have been put on the web 
site www.nrega.nic.in  under the heading 'Complaints'.  
To rectify corruption and harassment of beneficiari es under NREGA, Government has 
taken the following measures:  
(1) Transparency  
(i) Payment of wages through workers accounts in Banks/offices. So far 1,39,63,377 
accounts of NREGA workers in Banks/Post Offices have been opened.  
(ii) States have been advised to conduct social aud it of each and every work of 
NREGA within three months. Social Audit has been done in 76000 Gram Panchayats.  
(iii) A Citi2en Information Board has been introduced. This board is to be displayed at 
all prominent places. This will enable the local co mmunity to know the works 
being undertaken under NREGA and would also facilitate the process of spreading 
awareness about the programme.  
(2) Generating Awareness  
Various steps have been taken to generate awareness about NREGA. (i)  
Initiatives taken by State Government:  
(a)  Gram Sabhas and one day orientation of all Sarpanch es at the Block level 
have been held. 
(b)  leaflets and brochures in local language are being provided. 
(c)  Village camps have been organized by the District teams and Self help Groups 
and being associated in the awareness generation. 
(ii) Action taken by the Central Government:  
(a)  CAPART has been asked to provide training to the NGOs and Civil Society 
organisations associated in the awareness generation campaign. 
(b)  The Government of India has decided to introduce aw ards to be known as 
Rozgar Jagrookta Puraskar (Employment awareness awa rds) to recognize 
the outstanding contribution by the civil society organisations for promoting 
effective implementation of NREGA in different States of the country. 
(c)  Use of media, TV spots, radio jingles, advertisements films. 
(d) Development and dissemination of brochures and peoples prirners.  
(3) Vigilance and Monitoring  
(a) Implementation of NREG Act is monitored on regu lar basis. Vigilance and 
Monitoring Committees have been set up at State as well as district levels. Local 
MPs are the members of the district Vigilance and Monitoring Committees. Village 
level Vigilance and Monitoring Committees have also  been set up for local 
monitoring. Members of the Central Employment Guarantee Council also undertake 
field visits to various districts. National level M onitors and Area Officers visit 
various districts to over see the; progress of the Act. So far, NLMs have made 331 
visits to Phase I and Phase II districts.

Criteria for forming of SHGs under SGSY  
3219. SHRI SANJAY RAUT: Will the Minister of RURAL DEVELOPMENT be pleased to 
state:  
(a)  the criteria being followed while forming of Self-H elp-Groups (SHGs) under 
Swarnjayanti Gram Swarozgar Yojana (SGSY); and 
(b)  how many Self Help Groups are currently under the S GSY working, particularly in 
Maharashtra and the details of works undertaken by such SHGs? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURALDEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI 
SURYAKANTA PATIL): (a) The objective of the Swarnjayanti Gram Swarojgar Yojana (SGSY) is 
to bring the assisted families above the poverty li ne by ensuring appreciable increase lll 
incomes over a period of time. The criteria being followed while forming the Self-Help Groups 
are as below:  
1.  A self help group may consist of 10 to 20 persons. However, in difficult areas like 
desserts, hills and areas with scattered and sparse population and in case of minor 
irrigation and disabled persons, this number may be from 5—20. 
2.  Generally all members of the group should belong to families below the poverty 
line. However, if necessary, a maximum of 20% and in exceptional cases, where 
essentially required, upto a maximum of 30% of the members in a group may be 
taken from families marginally above the poverty li ne living contiguously with 
BPL Families and if they are acceptable to the BPL members of the group. 
3.  The group should actively participate in the manage ment and decision-making, 
such as devising a code of conduct, holding regular  meetings, building up a 
corpus through regular savings, evolving financial management norms, interest 
rates and procedures for sanctioning of the loans .etc. 
4.  The members in the group meetings should take all the loaning decisions through a 
participatory decision making process. 
5.  The group should operate a group account preferably in their service area bank 
branch. 
6.  The group should maintain simple basic records such as Minutes book, Attendance 
register, Loan ledger, General ledger, Cash book, Bank passbook and individual 
passbooks. 
(b) In the State of Maharashtra, under SGSY, since inception of the scheme from 1.4.1999, 
1,71,368 Self-Help Groups have been formed, out of which 1,05,875 SHGs have passed

quality maintenance at different level of production process (silkworm seed, cocoon and raw 
Silk production) for production of quality silk of international standard to compete in Global 
Markets has been made. As a part of this project, a scheme "Silk Mark" is launched through 
the Silk Mark Organisation of India (SMOI) under Central Silk Board for the products made 
from pure natural silk and guarantees the purity of silk products. It also plays an important 
role in brand promotion of Indian silk in deomestic and Export markets. Improving Research 
and Development and the effective transfer of techn ology at all staged, encouraging 
clustering of activities of reeling & weaving and s trengthening of linkages between the 
producers and industry and making amendment to the Central Silk Board Act [CSB 
(Amendment) Act 2006] to bring in quality norms in silkworm seed production to ensure 
improvement in silk productivity and quality are some other important measures taken by the 
Government of India.

Export of readymade garments  
3231. SHRI T.T.V. DHINAKARAN: Will the Minister of TEXTILES be pleased to state:  
(a)  whether export of readymade garments is not likely to achieve the target this year; 
(b)  if so, the reasons therefor; and 
(c)  the action taken to increase the exports? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF TEXTILES ( SHRI E.V.K.S. 
ELANGOVAN): (a) As per trends discernible from available exports statistics, exports of 
readymade garments is unlikely to achieve the targe ts of US$ 12065 million set for the 
Financial Year 2007-08.  
(b)  the shortfall in reaching the targets is being attributed by the apparel industry to the 
steep and consistent appreciation of the Indian rup ee vis-a-vis US dollar. In addition, the 
US market which accounts for 35% of Indian garment exports, has been sluggish since the 
beginning of 2007.    . 
(c)  Government has taken several measures to strengthen  the textiles industry, which 
will also have a positive impact on the exports of textiles and clothing. These measures are 
as follow: 
(i) The Technology Upgradation Fund Scheme (TUFS) h as been made operational 
from 1.4.1999 to facilitate the modermisation and upgradation of the sector. TUFS 
has been extended to cover the XI five year Plan pe riod. For the speedy 
modermisation of the textiles processing sector, Go vernment introduced, w.e.f. 
20.4.2005, a credit linked capital subsidy scheme @ 10% under TUFS, in addition 
to the existing 5% interest reimbursement.

(ii) The fiscal duty structure has been generally r ationalised to achieve growth and 
maximum value addition within the country. Except for mandatory excise duty on 
man-made filament yarns and man-made staple fibres, the whole value addition 
chain has been given the option of excise exemption.  
(iii) Import of specified textiles and garment mach inery has been allowed at a 
concessional rate of customs duty to encourage inve stment and to make our 
textiles product competitive in the global market. The cost of machinery has also 
been reduced through fiscal policy measures.  
(iv) Duty-free import upto 3% of actual export performance during the previous year, 
of 21 items of trimmings and embellishment items is allowed to garment exporters.  
(v) The entire textiles sector, except for man-made fibre and filament yarn was provided 
optional exemption from excise duty in 2004-05. In 2005-06 Central Value-added 
Tax (CENVAT) on Polyester Filament Yarn has been reduced from 24% to 16%. 
These modifications in fiscal levies aim at attract ing more investments for 
modernization of textile sector.  
(vi) To facilitate import of state of the art texti les machinery for manufacturing 
internationally competitive products in post quota regime, the customs duty on 
textile machinery has been brought down to 10% in 2005-06 except for 23 machinery 
items which attract Basic Customs Duty (BCD) of 15%.  
(vii) Government has launched the Debt Restructuring Scheme w.e.f. Sept., 2003 with 
the principal objective to permit banks to lend to the textiles sector at concessional 
rates of interest.

             Judgement giveny by the Supreme Court while interpreting the Delhi rent 
control Act, 1958  
SHRI SHANTARAM LAXMAN NAIK (Goa): Sir, there are se veral legislations in most of the 
States relating to the Rent Control Act in which a landlord can apply for recovery of 
•residential premises but not the premises which ar e given for commercial purposes. These 
are the special legislations which are passed by th e State Governments. Recently, Sir, the 
Supreme Court of India gave a ruling whereby landlords can apply for commercial premises 
also for their personal requirement. This type of a  provision is not there in most of the 
legislations. Even if these concessions are to be g iven to some people, considering their 
position in the society, considering that they are not financially well, then only the 
Legislature can amend the relevant statute to give such concessions. A court of law cannot 
amend a statute by way of interpretation. If this b ecomes a law throughout the country, 
there will be chaos in most of the Urban areas. Eve n those who do not require the 
commercial premises genuinely will apply for the co mmercial premises for their use and 
thousands of shopkeepers in most of the urban areas will be ousted. Therefore, Sir, there is 
a need that the Legislature must amend this. It is not a question of opposing any judgement. 
Court can pronounce a judgement, but citizens also have a right to express their views. 
Therefore, Sir, I would urge upon the Government that the Rent Control Act be amended to 
rectify this anomaly and to give certain concession s to those landlords whose commercial 
premises are given on rent but have some financial difficulties and, therefore, those premises 
can be taken by them for their personal requirement.

Flooding of Chinese mobiles in India without unique identification number or 
International mobile equipment identity  
SHRI M.V. MY SURAREDDY(Andhra Pradesh): Mr. Vice-Ch airman, Sir just now the 
Minister of Commerce and Industry said in this Hous e that there was no concern regarding 
imports and exports to China. In the last few month s, the Indian markets are flooded with 
mobile handsets, with cheap and high-end cutting Ch inese mobile technology.The problem 
with these handsets is, they are coming into the co untry without any unique identification 
number or international mobile equipment identity. As a result, these China made handsets 
are untraceable, and tracking of these sets is high ly impossible. Due to these reasons, the 
security agencies are expressing their concern that these sets would cause security threat to 
the country with this unique quality of invisiblene ss and untraceableness. As the mobile 
sets sold in India are mandated to have EAN and IMEI number so that in the case of theft or 
loss, these sets can be traced with the help of the se numbers, But in the case of Chinese 
handsets there are no such numbers. So, it is virtually impossible to know where and who is. 
using these mobile sets. As we all know, Mobile sets are playing a pivotal role in execution of 
various anti-social and terrorist activities. I would like to express my grave concern because if 
these sets are fallen in the hands of anti-social elements, gangsters, criminals and terrorists, 
with the unique quality of invisibleness, it would become virtually impossible for security 
agencies to track or trace the culprits and the ant i-social elements would perform their evil 
deeds without any hindrance. So these sets are real  threat to the security of the country. 
Hence 1 request the Government to ban import of Chi nese mobile handsets. If at all one 
vishes to import such sets, put a condition that on ly the handsets having EAN or IMEI 
numbers can be imported into the country. Thank you. 
Concern over kidnapping of Indian workers in Afghanistan  
SHRI BHARATKUM AR RAUT (Maharashtra): Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, I wish to raise an issue 
which is very urgent. The entire nation must have b een shocked to hear the news that yet 
another Indian has been kidnapped in Afghanistan. 1 wish to draw the attention of the entire 
House to this issue. It is really a matter of grave concern for all the Indians. An Indian worker, 
named Sarang Mohammad Naeem, who was working with a  Dubai-based firm in 
Afghanistan, while going back from his duty was abd ucted and till now he has not been 
traced. This is not a stray incident. There is a se ries of such incidents where Indians were 
attacked, abducted and often killed. It is a matter  of shame for us that we become silent 
spectators to such issues. Sir, Just a fortnight ago, when the Parliament was in recess, two 
Indians were killed in a suicide bomb attack,.Just before that there was another suicide attack 
in which two more Indians were killed. In November, 2006, Suryanarayana, a Telecome Engineer, 
who was working there, was kidnapped and was later found brutally murdered. What do we 
do? This is not all. Before that, in January 2005 also, a driver Mr. Kutty working with the Border 
Roads Organisation, was kidnapped and was later found murdered. 1 think we, the Indians 
are becoming soft targets of Talibanis or whichever organisation is operating in Afghanistan 
and we are being attacked. The Ministry of Exiernal Affiars and the Ministry of Home Affairs, 
should take it up and ensure that all those who are  working outside India, particularly in riot 
.orn or war torn areas like Afghanisatn should be g iven due protection. Otherwise, stop 
Indians from going to such areas. Why should we sen d our talent to be killed there? We 
have no-business or right to do that. I think, our External Affairs Ministry should take this very 
seriously and express our grave concern and also taken necessary measures.

US advice to India on the visit of Iranian President to India 
SHRIMATI BRINDA KARAT (West Bengal): Sir, on the occasion of the visit of the Iranian 
President to India, the US State Department has thought it fit to indulge in another act of gross 
interference in India's relations with other countries and has asked India to demand certain 
measures from Iran regarding its nuclear energy dev elopment. The statement reflects the 
imperialist arrogance of a self-appointed world policeman. We condemn this statement in the 
strongest terms. The External Affairs Spokesman has responded by saying that India does 
not require advice. (Interruptions) I am saying that he has responded that India does n ot 
require advice. That is good. It is an appropriate statement. But the point is: is it enough? It is 
not enough. We demand, Sir, that the US Ambassador should be summoned; and convey 
to him India's strong displeasure at the US stateme nt. This is necessary because the 
Manmohan Singh Government has, unfortunately, blemished record by voting twice against 
Iran in the IAEA. We have to give a clear message that India is not prepared to go along with 
the aggressive warmongering stance of the Bush Administration which threatens with military 
attacks against Iran. It is pertinent to recall that the Hyde Act passed by the US Congress has 
called upon India to cooperate with the United States to isolate Iran and also impose sanctions 
on Iran. This unsolicited advice, once again, highlights that the US considers India a Junior 
partner which it can pressurise to change its independent foreign policy. Sir, we believe that 
the Indian Government should recognise that Iran, as a signatory to the NPT, has the legal 
right to enrich nuclear fuel under international sa feguards. Therefore, the Iranian nuclear 
issue should be left to the IAEA to be dealt by them. We believe that the Indian Government 
should utilise the visit of the Iranian President to promote close cooperation with Iran and to 
get the Iran-Pakistan-India gas pipeline project finalised. I am sure, Sir, that I am reflecting the 
feeling of this House that the US Ambassador should be summoned to express our disapproval.

Need to promote Guwahati Airport as a regional connecting hub to South East 
Asian Nations 
SHRI BIRENDRA PRASAD BAISHYA (Assam): Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, I would draw the 
kind attention of the Government to the Guwahati Ai rport to be a regional hub for the air 
connectivity of the NER in terms of the Prime Minis ter's package of 1996. The Lokpriya 
Gopinath Bordoloi International Airport, Guwahati i s yet to be equipped for landing of 
Jumbo Aircraft due to inadequacy of requisite runway. Now only one flight is scheduled from 
Gopinath Bordoloi International Airport, Guwahati to Bangkok and people are not interested in 
North-Eastern Region for travelling to Bangkok only. Unless a full-fledged runway for landing 
of jumbo international aircraft is developed there seems to be no demand from other airlines. 
Such demand for international flights to various destinations in South East Asia like Tokyo, 
Singapore, etc. would come only after developing fu ll facilities of an internatieal airport like 
customs and immigration counter of international standards. I, therefore, urge on upon the 
Government to reiterate the earlier decision for making Guwahati Airport as the regional hub 
for the North Eastern Region and create all facilities for customs and immigration along with 
requisite infrastructure for cargo handling, aero b ridges, etc., in a separate international 
terminal building to encourage export activities from the region in view of 'Look East Policy'. 
Thank you.

Concern over the misrable condition of Tribals of Dangs in Gujarat  
SHRI PRAVEEN RASHTRAPAL (Gujarat): Sir, a recent report by Shri A.P. Ravani, Former 
Chief Justice, Rajasthan High Court which is published by Gujarat Foundation for Development 
Alternatives' Vadodara, Gujarat State has proved th at Bhil Rajas who fought British and 
Gaekwad Army, before 1947, are in rags today and get annual political pension of Rs. 21- to 
Rs. 1000/- from present rulers. The Dangs did not form part of British India. They have never 
been conquered or annexed by the Government nor they have been ceded. 
In view of the above, hon. Home Minister may clarify the following issues:— 
(i) whether any merger agreement was taken from the Tribal Chief of Dangs? 
(ii) If no, why the same was not taken? 
(iii) Is it true that the Tribal Chiefs had passed resolution objecting to the merger with 
the Bombay Province? 
(iv) When was the question of rights and privileges of the Chief and Naiks decided? 
(v) How the Chiefs were made political pensioners instead of ex-rulers? 
(vi) Who collects the land revenue in Dangs? 
(vii) What is the total amount collected till 31.03.2007 towards land revenue? 
(viii) How much from the above collection is paid to Dang Tribal Chiefs? 

160    Special [RAJYA SABHA] Mentions  
(ix) Is the Home Ministry aware about the letter da ted 22.3.2005.from Accountant 
General, according to which the Dangs Reserve Fund has a balance of Rs. 
2,21,52,000 and? 
(x) What is the proposal from Government of India a nd Government of Gujarat to 
utilise the above fund for upliftment of Dangs people? 
SHRI SILVIUS CONDPAN (Assam) Sir, I associate myself with the Special Mention made by 
Shri Praveen Rashtrapal. 
MS. SUSHILATIRIYA(Orrisa-): Sir, I associate myself with the Special Mention made by Shri 
Praveen Rashtrapal. 
Need to take immediate steps to address the problems being faced by Indian workers 
stranded in Ajaokuta Steel City of Nigeria  
SHRI SAMAN PATHAK. (West Bengal): Sir, it is a mater of grave concern that over 80 
Indians, some with families mostly from Kerala, Tam il Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Kamataka, 
Maharashtra, Orissa have been stranded in the Ajaok uta Steel City in Nigeria for the last 
ten days after the federal Government revoked the d eal that gave control of two State-
owned steel firms to Global Infrastructure (Nigeria) Ltd. for 'asset stripping'. GINL is part of 
the Global Steel Holdings Ltd. The stranded Indians include 47 employees of the Ajaokuta 
Steel Company Ltd. and 20 of the Nigerian Iron Ore Mining Company. Most of the personnel 
held up in the city include cooks, technicians, boi ler operators, chargemen and general 
managers are virtually under house arrest in their quarters, two kilometres from the steel 
city. Armed policemen and security officials of the  company were reportedly guarding 
them, fearing attack from the local Ebira youth. Mo st of the employees had not been paid 
salaries for nine months and 'living allowance' for  six months. Hence, I urge upon the 
Government to look into the matter. 
SHRI MATILAL SARKAR (Tripura): Sir, I associate myself with the Special Mention made 
by Shri Saman Pathak.

Demand for extending anti-dumping duty on Raw Silk for another Five Years  
SHRIG1REESH KUMAR SANGHI (Andhra Pradesh): Sir, the sericulture and the weaving 
industry have just stabilized in the State of Andhr a Pradesh during the last 4-5 years. The 
State, in association with the Central Silk Board, Ministry of Textile, has made plans to invest 
Rs. 700 crores in the next five years to produce in ternational grade raw silk which will 
compete with Chinese imported raw silk. The domesti c industry is gearing up to meet the 
demand and supply gap. Since the Chinese export prices are unpredictable and capable of 
bringing down our prices which will affect our sericulture sector, it is, therefore, necessary to 
take all possible steps to safeguard the interests of sericulture farmers and domestic industry. 
As the sericulture activity is rural-based and undertaken by marginal farmers and reelers who 
belong to weaker/minority sections of the society, it is necessary to extend the anti-dumping 
duty by another five years. As the anti-dumping dut y on raw silk had expired in January, 
2008, various associations, with the help of Central Silk Board and the State Governments, 
have petitioned to the Ministry of Commerce for extension of the same. 
1, therefore, urge upon the Government of India to kindly extend the anti-dumping duty, as 
also demanded by the Government of Andhra Pradesh, by another five years to safeguard 
the interests of sericulture farmers not only in An dhra Pradesh, but in the entire country. 
Thank you 
Demand to stop the proposed Sale of Bharat Mata Theatre, Lalbag, Mumbai 
SHRI MANOHAR JOSHI (Maharashtra): Sir, the Bharat Mata Theatre at Lalbag, Mumbai, in 
the National Textiles Corporation complex has been a symbol of Marathi culture, the only 
theatre exhibiting Marathi films. 
The NTC has initiated legal proceedings for the evi ction of present occupant. They 
intend to sell this property by way of open tender. This will ultimately lead to closure of this 
theatre. 
The' aforesaid decision of NTC will gravely hurt the Marathi sentiments. 
I demand that the proposed sale of Bharat Mata Thea tre may be nut on hold. Further 
steps be taken to lease the theatre to the present occupant so that the exhibition of Marathi 
films could continue in the interest of Marathi culture. 
SHRI SANJAY RAUT (Maharashtra): Sir, I associate myself with the sentiments expressed 
by the hon. Member, Shri Manohar Joshi.

THE VICE CHAIRAMAN((PRO.P.J.KURIEN):Please conclude. 
SHRIMATIBRINDA KARAT (West Bengal): Sir, I am happy that I have this occasion to support 
the Bill to make JMIPER an Institute of national im portance, and I also have the occasion to 
congratulate the Health Minister for acepting the major amendments which I had moved in the 
last session. Sir, those were not my personal amendments. Those amendments, came up as a 
result of the big struggle of the people of Puduche rry and the,academic community of 
Puducherry. Therefore, it was only a reflection of a joint effort of those in the Institute and the 
people of Puducherry who felt that the drafft which  had been placed before Parliament in 
December would have actually taken away the uniqueness of this Institute in Puducherry. 
Sir, there wer four major issues. The first was that today it is unique in the sense that it is 
open for the poor and it helps in providing medical service to them. I am very happy that the 
Minister has included that amendment in the Act itself and not just the rules. It is important. I 
have absolutely no question about the intentions of  the Minister when he said in the last 
Session. "I will include all mis in the Rules". I knew that as far as the Minister is concerned, 
there is no issue there, but the question it, it is  our job to institutionalise the rights of the 
poor for access to medical treatement, and, that is why, Sir, I had insisted that it should come 
in the Act The second point is, the people and the families of Puducherry have that benefit 
that they can get their children admitted into Puducherry at a much lower cost than in any of 
the other Institutes. It is important because we know now today that medical institutions and 
medical education cost so much money that it is ver y, very difficult for a bright student 
coming from a poor family to be able to access that  education and, the before, we were 
extermely concerned that this provision must be the re. There was some legal opinion 
saying. No, it is not possible; if it is there, it is going to be struck down,etc." But I am really 
happy that today, I won't say a precedent, but, certainly, I will say that an example has 
 

166   Government [RAJYA SABHA] Bill  
been set by the Minister by including this aspect of the local recruitment linked with the aspect of 
control of fees to those of other Central Institutions. Sir, both these things linked together will 
provide access to poorest sections of our people to enable them to get their children, who have 
been deprived through no fault of theirs but because of an exploitative system, have accest to 
higher education, higher medical education. Therefore, this is a very important aspect. 
The other aspect, Sir, is that of employees' rights . We know that if we want sustained 
advancement of any insitution, it is extremely important to have the cooperation of the entire 
community of that institution. I was extremely concerned that the issues of the employees in the 
Institute may not have been protected in the earlier draft as they should have been. There was a 
penalty clause regarding the principles of natural justice for an employee to appeal against any 
punishment awarded to him. There was a wording and a formulation there, which may have been very 
damaging and could have caused a wrong precedent for the rights of the employees. That has been 
removed and it is also a fact that as far as the transfer or opting to the Central Government is 
concerned, the employees will have to study the rules before they take such a decision. Although it 
is a convention of Parliament that rules should be framed within six months of a Bill being enacted 
into law, we all know that sometimes it does take unfortunately a much longer than that period.

Discussion on the working of the Ministry of Labour and Employment  
SHRI D. RAJA (TAMIL NADU): Sir, I rise to initiate the discussion on the working of the 
Ministry of Labour and Employment. At the outset, I would like to congratulate the Minister, 
my dear friend, Mr. Oscar Fernandes, who is more ea sily approachable and more 
accessible. Having said this, I must say that the Government is not an 'individual' rather it is 
'collective' entity. Sir, the UPA Government came t o power with six principles for 
governance. 
One of these six basic principles, according to the Common Minimum Programme of the 
UPA Government, is to enhance welfare and well being of farmers, labourers and workers, 
particularly, those in the unorganised sector, and assure a secure future for their families in 
other respects. This is one of the six basic princi ples outlined in the Common Minimum 
Programme of the UPA Government. 
Now, in this background, we will have to review the  performance of the Ministry. I have 
some statistics with me. The Annual Budget of the M inistry was Rs. 971 crores in the year 
2003-04. It was increased to Rs. 1045.77 crores in the year 2004-05. That was the year 
when the UPA Government came to office. 
As far as this amount in subsequent years is concerned, in 2005-06, it was Rs. 1311.03 
crores; in 2006-07, it was Rs. 1,643.56 crores; in 2007-08, it was Rs. 1,897.25 crores, and, 
for the year 2008-09, this amount is Rs. 2,498.01 c rores. There is no substantial increase 
in the Budget under the UPA Government for the Mini stry of Labour and Employment. 
Even then, it is the question of how the Ministry f unctions. In this context, I must draw the 
attention of the House, the Standing Committee on L abour has submitted its Report. The 
recommendations, which have been made, are unanimou s. Whether the UPA 
Government is going to accept these recommendations ? It is not the question of just 
acceptance of the recommendations of the Standing C ommittee. Whether the UPA 
Government is going to act or not on these recommen dations? We have the Chief Labour 
Commissioner. How this institution functions, I am saying because this is the institution 
which is supposed to look after the implementation of the labour laws and all issues 
related to the labour. I think, there is a need to strengthen this institution. The money, 
even though it is not a very substantial increase, has to be utilised to the optimum to see 
the Central Labour Commissioner and his entire establishment functions with a capacity. 
Sir, when we look at the functioning of labour and employment, I would like to draw the 
attention of the House, in 1970s and 80s when the GDP was growing at an average of 4 per 
cent, the employment growth was around 2 per cent. Now, when the Government claims 
that the GDP is growing at close to 9 per cent, emp loyment growth is only 3.5 per cent. 
This oniy shows that the economic growth is not Accompanied by employment opportunity. I 
do not know how the UPA Government is going to explain this sort of growth. Moreover,

Now, I come, to the next point, that is, the fifth schedule of the Industrial Disputes Act, 
which deals with the unfair labour practices. The m atters with regard to managements 
indulging in the unfair labour practice have to be reported to the Government. Then, the 
Government will-take action against the management and, if they find it right, they may file 
prosecution also. But I say that an aggrieved party itself can be given powers. Why should 
the Government come into picture? If I feel that my  employer is adopting unfair labour 
practices, I must have a right to go to the labour court or the industrial tribunal and file a 
petition that the management is resorting to unfair labour practices, removes people without 
any notice, without compensation, etc. This way I can prove my point and win the case. But, 
today, if I want to go to court, I have to seek permission from the Government. Why are there 
so many powers with the Government? Every power has  been kept with the Government. 
The powers with regard to unfair labour practice are with the Government; clarifications have to 
be given by the Government, and so on and so forth.  This way, neither the Government is 
able to function efficiently, nor the things are go ing to be implemented. Even the minimum 
wages have not been implemented by the Government. There are a number of instances. 
Twenty thousand workers are employed in the Chhatis garh Steel Industry. Out of this, 
nineteen thousand are contract workers and only one thousand are permanent workers. This 
is the state of affairs in a steel company! This is  the situation. Nobody is there to care of it. 
So, I say why don't you give more liberty to trade unions so that they are able to solve 
problems. Take the case of SEZs. You say that there is no restriction on the formation of trade 
unions and workers can represent their grievances. But in all the multi-national industries or 
SEZ industries, if one wants to form a union one can't form it. The State Government do not 
want to register a union and the Central Government does not have a say in the matter. The 
State Government says that in the SEZ units, there is one Industrial Director, you may 
register your trade union there. But he does not register it. One has to go to the High Court. 
The High Court will take ten years to give a decision. So, in such cases, the management is 
adopting anti-labour and anti-trade union policies. Similarly, multinationals are also adopting 
anti-labour policies. All the trade union leaders are dismissed and discharged. No protection is 
there. We want a protection from the illegal action of a management and the Government is not 
able to provide that protection. At least, strengthen the trade union movement so that we can 
protect the workers interest. That is my submission . I want to say that today there are no 
strikes, but a number of industries have been closed down. You may notice that in the private 
sector, a number of industries have been closed down. Around 5-10 lakh small scale industries 
have been closed down at a number of places. Why did it happen? It happened because the 
contract system is prevailing. They close an indust ry here and open it somewhere else. 
They engage all the workers on contract basis. They employ cheap labour and exploit them, 
the management is closing down the industry. But, we say, that after closing the industry, or 
before closing the industry, you ask the workers who are employed in that industry, whether 
they want to run that industry or not. You have to tell them that you are closing down and 
that their jobs will be taken away. The trade union s and the workers may be inquired 
whether they are ready to take over this industry and run it on their own for 

Government [23 APRIL 2008] Bill    185 
employment sake. If you give them this option, then , you will find that a number of trade 
unions will be ready to take over. Sir, we took over one textile mill in Surat. We took it over 10 
years back, and still we are running it. We guaranteed employment to the workers. We are 
continuing as a trade union on cooperative basis, a nd we are running that spinning mill. 
Similarly, there are a number of other trade unions who would want to run the industry if the 
management decides to close down and remove thousan ds of workers. But, nobody is 
asking the trade unions. If we ask them, they say, "In what way are you concerned with that? 
You are trade union worker; you are only a worker, you cannot ask this quesiton." I do not 
have a locus standi. If you make me a shareholder, then, I will have a locus standi. I can take 
over the industry. I can run the industry. Trade union workers are not only demand-oriented 
or job-oriented, but they want to safeguard the int erests of the workers. They want of 
safeguard the jobs of the workers. We want to play a role in the management also. This is my 
submission. 
My next point is about skill development programme. We suggested to the Government 
that a Workers' Technical University should be set up. All the workers should be given a 
guarantee that their children will be trained and educated in the workers' technical university. 
That was the demand we made before the human Resource Development Minister. He agreed 
to it in principle. We say that a workers' technica l university should be set up and all the 
organised and unorganised sector workers should be given a guarantee that their children 
will be imparted education at cheaper rate or free of cost. All the facilities, like accommodation 
etc. should be given to them so that their children can also become engineers, scientists or 
some other officer. This dream of the worker should be fulfilled. This is my submission. 
Lastly, 1 want to say that we are with the Government. We want to give our full cooperation to 
the Government. We want to support the Government. We are supporting the Government, but, 
labour reforms are required. Labour reforms should be implemented. The employer is also 
asking for labour reforms. We are also demanding fo r the same. The employer wants to 
increase profits. We want development of personality of the working class so that they can 
be protected; their jobs can be protected and their earnings can be protected. Therefore, we 
want to say that reforms are required under the present situation of globalised economy and 
competition. You may see that today in the UK, they  have got trade unions. Trade union 
movement was once a consolidated thing; But, unfort unately, in India, we have a divided 
house on the trade unions issue. Otherwise, in the UK, the Labour Party came into existence 
because of the trade unions. The Labour Party was b rought to power by the trade unions. 
And Labour Party is able to rule the UK even today also. If the trade union movement is 
consolidated and made strong, then, it can become an economic power and political power 
for the working class movement. Therefore, I appeal to the Government to see that the trade 
union movement is protected and workers are protected. Thank you, Sir.

SHRI T.K. RANGARAJAN (Tamil Nadu): Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, the Labour Ministry is 
very important for the entire workforce and 62.57 m illion organised and millions of 
unorganised sector workforce have to be protected b y this Ministry. Therefore, we are 
sorry that the Ministry is so marginalized. In toda y's neo-liberal world, we have more 
corporate welfare than labour welfare. Sir, though the Minister is committed with good 
intentions, the Central Government has initiated st eps to bring the rights of workers and 
their defence to the centre-stage by sidelining them and pushing them back; and the Minister 
is helpless. 
Sir, the Non-Plan expenditure remains practically u nchanged. It means that they have 
clearly violated all norms. The enforcement machine ry is inadequate. In the last Indian 
Labour Conference, it was unanimously concluded that all vacant posts in the enforcement 
machinery should be filled up. But the views of the  Labour Ministry in this matter have not 
been taken into account. I am forced to say that th is Government is promoting violation of 
labour laws. 
I don't want to go through this entire book. It giv es a lot of statistics which are not 
satisfactory. But I do want to tell this House that  in the case of Beedi Workers' Welfare 
Fund, out of Rs. 230 crores, they have spent only Rs. 226 crores. In the case of rehabilitation 
of bonded labour, the Budget is Rs. 1.8 crores and they have spent only Rs. 1.5 crores. In 
the case of improvement of working conditions of the child and women labour, it has been 
cevised from Rs. 171 crores to Rs. 153 crores. With regard to the welfare of SCs, STs and 
OBCs, the allocation of money is nominal which can' t be accepted. If you go through the 
Report of the Standing Committee on Labour, Chapter -Ill, Report on Demands for Grants 
2007-08, the Ministry in a written reply has stated as follows: 
"Holding of Lok Adalt:..The reason for less expendi ture is due to the fact that the posts of 
Presiding Officers of some of the CCITs were lying vacant, as such Lqk Adalats could not 
be held." construction of houses for beedi workers and low-income occupation clusters; the 
reason for nil expenditure is attributed to non-app roval of the scheme on the Plan side. 
However, the scheme continues to be operated on the Non-Plan side. 
Rehabilitation of bonded labour; the reason for les s expenditure is attributed to non-
receipt of complete proposals from the State Governments. 
The Committee are constrained to note that out of m ore than 40 crores of workforce in 
this country, the total membership of the EPFO, as on 31st March, is only 4.6 crores, both 
in the exempted and unexampted sectors, which is just 10.74 per cent of the total workforce. 
The Committee are least satisfied with the sorry state of affairs. 
The Committee note with concern that the arrears du e for recovery are continuously 
mounting, year after year, against the defaulting establishments. 
On ESI, the Committee are constrained to note that the ESI facilities are not available 
in all the States and Union Territories, even after 60 years of its coming into force. 
The DGMS has the total sanctioned strength of 978 p ersons with 741 in position, thus

a shortfall of 237 in different categories as on 1.1.2007. 
The Committee are constrained to note that there ha s been steady decline in the number of 
inspections and inquiries conducted during the last three years. The prime reason for decline in  
the number of inspections and inquiries has been re portedly due to the shortage of frontline 
inspecting officers.
