The Committee note with concern that there are 2.57  crore construction workers and 
4.9 million beedi workers in this country. Sir, four years have passe d after the UPA 
Government adopted the National Common Minimum Prog ramme. However, most of the 
programmes remained unimplemented, so far as the wo rking class is concerned. It is 
difficult to predict how far the comitments given i n the CMP will be implemented in the rest 
of the one-year period. 
Then attack on labour rights. As I said, the welfar e of the corporate management is the 
concern of the Government. The Economic Survey, 200 7-08 has suggested reviewing of 
labour laws and labour market regulations. This has been the consistent demand projected in 
different meetings and seminars organised by FICCI and CII. The fact is, as we could read 
from our experience, the labour laws are already un der the neo-liberal offensive in this 
country. We are told that we are in second generati on of neo-liberal policy regime. Three 
main aspects of that regime, the framework of which has been worked out by the international 
agencies, are: total liberalisation in financial sector; complete overhauling of labour laws and 
complete liberalisation and deregulation of trade. All these three aspects make an Impact on 
the rights and livelihood of the working people. An y attempt to amend the labour laws, an 
exercise the Government is willing to do in favour of capitalists, will result in deregulation of 
labour market affecting the working class. This is promoted as a matter of policy by those in 
governance at the Centre and in many States. The reason mooted is "investment friendliness". 
The inspection machinery is made defunct in many States, through official orders as also the 
grievance settlement machinery. A system of self-certification by employers on compliance of 
labour laws has been introduced by the Centre and some States. 
Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act is t he most consistently violated labour 
law. Other labour laws such as Minimum Wages Act, P ayment of Wages Act, Industrial 
Disputes Act do not escape violations. All these fa vour non-enforcement of labour laws 
regarding wages, labour rights, health, safety, etc. 
"Fixed Term Employment" category introduced by the NDA Government meant to 
institutionalise casual labour system in place of p ermanent work and avoid obligations 
under the contract Act and the Industrial Disputes Act is being resorted to despite assurance 
of the Labour Minister to rescind it. 
Violation has got two dimensions. One is the non-im plementation of basic labour laws 
and, two curbing trade union rights to prevent fighting those tendencies. For example, Sir, as 
a trade unionist, I find that there is a total coll apse of labour legislation in the country. Just 
around Delhi, in Gazhiabad, Faridabad, Western U.P., Haryana, Punjab, Rajasthan and Madhya 
Pradesh, several units are forcing the workers to w ork twelve hours a day without paying 
any over-time allowance. Some State Governments are  conniving in the violation of law. 
Some of them have issued circulars that the factory inspectors should not inspect factories 
without the permission of the Secretary, Labour Dep artment. Such violation of laws has to 
be noted by the Labour Minister and a strong intervntion is needed. 
Even the MNCs are not bothered about respecting the laws of this land. In Tamil Nadu, 
the Hyundai management refused to hold discussions with the registered trade union. Instead, 
they have transferred the elected office bearers, dismissed the Union President, Joint Secretary 
and others and transferred many of them. More than hundred workers have been charge-
sheeted.

I am surprised to note that the Textile Minister has openly made a statement proposing 12 
hours work a day in garment factories, totally viol ating the labour laws. It should be noted 
here that in the policy reform options of the Economic Survey, 2007-08, under the heading of 
the Factories Act, it has been suggested to increase the work-week to 60 hours from 48 hours 
and the daily limit to 12 hours and to meet seasona l demand through overtime. I would 
request the hon. Labour Minister to make a categorical statement when he replies whether 
this is a Cabinet decision or Government of India's policy. I request him, through the Chair, 
that he must make a categorical statement here. 
Now, an example of how a Government department func tions and how they treat their 
own employees ~ five of the office bearers of Akash vani and Doordarshan Administrative 
Staff Association are now on an indefinite fast in front of the Akashwani Bhawan, New 
Delhi. They are agitating for the past eight years. They had got favourable replies from the 
then Minister of Information and Broadcasting, Shri Jaipal Reddy and the present Minister of 
Information and Broadcasting, Shri Priyaranjan Dasm unsi also; I spoke to him even 
yesterday. But, for the past eight years the matter has not been settled. Who is the culprit? 
This is how the Ministry is treating its own employ ees. I request the Minister of settle their 
demands immediately and save their lives. Sir,, the  Sixth Commission openly 
recommended abolition of Group 'D' posts and getting those jobs done through outsourcing. 
In several Departments of the Government, perennial nature of jobs are already outsourced. 
In Public Sector Undertakings, one-third of jobs ar e reduced through Voluntary Retirement 
Scheme, and, in their places, contract workers are working. 
Sir, in the Neyveli Lignite Corporation, the contract workers, working in perennial nature of 
jobs, are demanding regularisation of their jobs. The Minister has given them a favourable 
reply. Let us wait and see how the Minister is goin g to deal with these workers. There are 
thousands of private companies where overwhelming m ajority of jobs are done by the 
contract workers. Unfortunately, the Government is introducing the new Pension Scheme 
with an attempt to invest in pension fund in speculative market. It is giving low interest on PF 
and small savings.

authority. ...(Interruptions)... Sir, what happens is that the Ministers which are headed by

the Cabinet Minister, they do not listen to the advice of the Labour Ministry. They do not

care even to attend the Indian Labour Organisation. You must come and sit there. As a result of the 
casual approach, the Labour Ministry, the Indian Labour Conference, and the Standing Committee 
have been converted into a debating society. There are 35 Tripartite Committees under the Ministry 
of Labour but a majority of them have not held their meeting during the year 2007. This made a 
mockery of the tripartite consultations. The NCMP promises to consult labour and trade unions 
on all the major issues but inpractice the Government has given up proper consultation in its 
true spirit. 
Sir, every one is aware of the high prices of the essential commodities in the country but this is 
not reflected in the Consumer Price Index prepared by the Labour Bureau under the Ministry of 
Labour. All the Central Trade Unions unanimously opposed the introduction of the new index series 
with 2001 as the base year. This series is fraudulent and several manipulations are taking place 
to keep the index down and workers are defrauded of their legitimate Dearness Allowance to the 
tune of thousands of crores of rupees every month due to this Index fraud. The demand of the 
Indian Trade Unions to appoint an index Review Committee like a tripartite committee was set up 
in 1978 to go into the entire question of complication of index is not being accepted by the 
Government. 
Sir, I want to know from the Labour Ministry as to why the legitimate demands of the trade unions are 
not being considered by the Government. A Constitutional Committee, which is not on the lines of 
1978 Committee, does not serve the purpose at all. 
The sickness of the industry is increasing all over the country but the Labour Ministry has not 
found any mechanism to revive potentially volatile sick industries. A large number of people are 
unemployed and this number is swelling every month but the Ministry, which is having employment 
portfolio, has practically no role to play in employment generation. Regarding child labour, I would 
submit that the allocation of money is very small and even that is not spent properly. For example, 
Kerala is having the lowest number of child labour. Why? It is because nobody wants his or her child 
to be a child labour. Everybody wants to see that his son or daughter is educated and employed 
elsewhere. But the point is what is happening. More than 50 per cent of the unorganised workers 
are drawing Rs. 20 daily as wage as stated by the Arjun Sengupta Commission. That is way the 
children are working as child labourer. In Kerala, the minimum wage is the highest in India. So, the 
number of children who are working as child labourers is very small. Secondly, in Tamil Nadu two 
days back, it was stated in the Assembly that dropout rate has come down due to supply of eggs 
for the Mid-day Meal Scheme. They have given the statistics. In 2002-03, the dropout rate at primary 
school level was 12 per cent. In 2006-07, the dropout rate came down to 2 per cent. Sir, 72 lakh 
children got the benefit. The dropout rate has come down because of the correct policies and 
approach of the DMK Government in Tamil Nadu. So, I would request the Central Government to 
give money to every State to protect children from the clutches of child labour. Sir, many State 
Governments do not have revenue like Tamil Nadu. So, the Central Government has to provide 
funds to them. 
Finally, I, therefore, urge upon the hon. Labour Minister to review the labour policy of the UFA 
Government during the last four years and take expeditious steps to adhere to the NCMP and 
implement all the assurances given in the NCMP. The labour policy of  the

he realizes the gravity of the situation and take f irm steps to ensure implementation of the 
commitments made in the NCMP. Thank you.

SHRI  N.R. GOVINDARAJAR (Tamil Nadu): *I thank the Chair for giving me an opportunity to speak 
in this august House on the performance of the Ministry of Labour and Employment. I would like 
to put forth my views on behalf of All India Anna Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam. 
Sir, if you would ask me whether this Ministry has done anything worthwhile to benefit the 
people, my answer would be a big "No". No plan has been evolved properly to benefit the 
working class. I am pained to point out that unemployment problem has increased manifold 
in the last ten years and job opportunities have not been created. In computer technology we 
have made new strides. But enough of job opportunit ies have not been created. Barring 
Information Technology other sectors have-not given  rise to increase in job opportunities. 
There is a law of the land that prohibits the exploitation called child labour. Children under 14 
are not supposed to be engaged to work in factory u nits, industrial units, maines and other 
work places. But what prevails is to the contrary. 
We legsilated as early as in 1986 an Act abolishing child labour preventing children below 
14 from being employed in work places. But there are lacunae in the implementation of that 
Act which remains merely on paper. National Sample Survey conducted in the year 2001 
mentions that about 1 crore and 20 lakh children ar e found in the shackles of child labour. 
How sordid is that? There is a law in place but children are still exploited in work places. 
Children must not get affected mentally and physica lly. They must not be exploited for 
socio-economic reasons. The children must not be deprived of their childhood and robbed of 
their rights. We must bear in mind that we would be harming a set of future generation if we 
harm the interests of our children rendered as child labour. National Child Welfare Schemes are 
there in place for the past 20 years under the aegi s of the Ministry of Labour and 
Employment. There can not be any shameful thing oth er than the condition that there are 1 
crore and 20 lakh children left in the lurch as child labour. It is also a matter of shame that just 
4 lakh children have benefited out of the Welfare S cheme aimed at them. In the task force 
report for the Eleventh Five Year Plan it was recom mended that child labour must be 
identified and provided with educational facilities. Unfortunately the Union Government has not 
accepted that recommendation. Under 21(A) of the Ch ild Labour Prohibition Act, it is 
incumbent on the part of the State Government to ensure that no child under 14 years of age 
is engaged as child labour and it is also the responsibility of the State Government to provide 
educational facilities to those children. Under Art icle 204 of our Constitution, State must 
ensure that children must not be employed in hazard uous industries. But still the number of 
child labour in such units are on the increase. It is a disheartening fact that such children are 
taken to such hazarduous units by their own parents . This Government and this Ministry 
has not arrested this trend. A survey report says t hat about 65,700 children are engaged in 
cotton cultivation in Tamil Nadu and they are under  paid. Hazarduous match industries and 
fire-works manufacturing units in Sivakasi in Tamil Nadu are still engaging children and pay 
them meagre wages. We do not have any information a bout any action on the part of the 
Union Government to liberate and rehabilitate the c hildren employed as child labour in 
Sivakasi.

In thirteen districts in Tamil Nadu this Child Labour (Prevention) Act is in force. It must be 
enforced in all the districts. I would like to appe al to this House to impress upon the 
Government the need to help save children and their childhood. Funds allocated to implement 
this is inadequate. I also urge upon the Union Mini stry of Labour to monitor the enforcing 
and implementation of this in Tamil Nadu. 
Human Rights Commission has stated that there are about four crore people live a bonded 
labour. The survey report also says that about one crore and fifty lakhs of children lead their 
lives as bonded labour. I urge upon the Ministry to  furnish details about the action taken in 
this regard to restore and rehabilitate the children who are toiling as bonded labour. In all the 
29 districts in which this Act is in force, Government must come forward to extend all possible 
assistance to children to get education and rehabilitation. 
Let me come to Contract Labour. Their conditions ar e much to be desired. We proudly 
claim unashamedly that we have achieved 9% growth r ate when the contract labour are 
getting a raw deal. Poor salary and absence of social security threaten their future and they 
live below poverty line. Not only the Centre, the S tate Government has also increased the 
number of contract labour. It is painful to note th at the number of contract labour has 
increased in Tamil Nadu to the tune of about 6.52%. 
There is an uneven growth. The rich and poor divide is widening. On the one side we have 
computer professionals earning in lakhs but on the other side we have unskilled labour left 
in the lurch with meagre wages. Right to work must be made a fundamental right. In the 
absence of it the Union Government brought about Na tional Rural Employment Guarantee 
Act. We were happy about it for a while. But the CA G report says that the job guarantee 
scheme is a failure as there is no proper implementation. 
This scheme was introduced in 330 districts with an  allocation of Rs. 1200 crores which 
can get only eighteen days of work per individual. 40,587 children in Uttar Pradesh had 
applied to be the beneficiaries under this scheme. But all of them could not get the benefit 
and proper records are not maintained. Auditing off icials have stated that they do not get 
any detail about the spending in Tamil Nadu. 
I urge upon the Union Minister to provide details about the fund allocation to Tamil Nadu for 
the National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme and the auditors' reports about the 
way in which they have been spent along with details about any possible diversion of funds 
in the last two years. 
About 70% of our population are in the unorganized sector. They get less than Rs. 20 per 
day. I would like to draw the attention of this House to their plight as they live below poverty 
line. Only 23% of the labour class are in position to buy essential goods. The remaining 77% 
of the labour class are left to fend for themselves. Only 2% of bank loans go to these people 
in the unorganized sector. A separate fund for the welfare of the workers in the unorganized 
sector must be set up. In 1993-94 the unemployment rate was 6.1% and it had increased to 
8.3% in 2003-04. What was 9.5% then in the agricultural sector had increased to 15.3%.

SHRI N.R. GOVINDARAJAR: I shall take only one minute. 
Sir, People in the lower ladder and the middle clas s people have been greatly 
affected. They Government are claiming that job opportunities would incerase in the wake of 
economic liberalization, increased foreign Direct I nvestment and the creation of Special 
Economic Zones. But the poor remain poor and the ri ch and poor divide is widening. A 
private steel . mill could increase its production five fold that is 500% in fourteen years. 
Recently I read about this. Can it be an achievemen t? But in the fourteen years more 
than fifty per cent of the employee-workers were hugely exploited. I would like to sound a 
word of caution that it would be dangerous to incre ase Foreign Direct Investment and 
Special Economic Zones. 
This Government must contemplate about the good mea sures that were brought 
about by our Puratchi Thalaivi Amma when she was Ch ief Minister of Tamil Nadu..She 
brought about a social security measure to help the  workers in the rural areas. Unlike 
many other States including States ruled by the com munists the transport workers 
were not getting pensionary benefits. It was only our leader Puratphi Thalaivi Amma who 
extended pensionary benefit to transport workers in  whole of India. Contract workers 
must be regularized as it was done by our leader. M inimum wages must be fixed to 
extend benefit to the workers in the unorganized se ctor. Impressing upon the Union 
Government to emulate our leader in introducing and  implementing welfare measures 
for the working class, let me conclude. Thank You.

UPA Government. Some people said that the building and construction workers' legislation 
came at the time of Deva Gowda Government, which is not correct. It came in the form of an 
Ordinance which was promulgated in the year 1995 on 3rd December. Ultimately, the Bill was 
passed in 1996 and rules were framed and laid in Parliament in 1997. That is the fact which I 
want to mention here. Not only this, I would also l ike to put on record that most of the 
legislations relating to labour, whatever is the figure, 147 or 148, have been enacted during 
the regime of Congress Government. There have been many Governments; there have been 
many Prime Ministers. I do not want to name anybody but there is not a single legislation for the 
protection of the workers in the country, which they can claim to have enacted when they were 
in power. Sir, when the NDA was there, reforms have been there; when the UPA is here, reforms 
are also here but the only difference between the NDA and the UPA is that the NDA tried to 
amend the Labour Laws, the Industrial Disputes Act, the Contract Labour Act, but could not 
do so. On the other hand, till today, the UPA Government has protected the labour class and 
has not done anything that has proved to be detrimental to the interests of the workers. 
Sir, if we take the example of the Bonus Act, it was amended during the tenure of Prime 
Minister Narasimha Rao in the Congress Government, and, the base level was raised from 
1600 to 2500. Now, again, the Bonus Act is amended when Shri Oscar Fernandes is the 
Labour Minister and Shri Manmohan Singh is the Prim e Minister. Not only that, when the 
Bonus Act was amended at the time of Narasimha Rao Government, it was implemented with 
retrospective effect. It was a historic decision. 
Sir, coming to the interest rate on Provident Fund, an issue mentioned by Panyji, who is 
not here now, I would like to say that he has forgotten that when the NDA Government was 
there, they could not take a decision on it. They are trying to make it eight per cent. Under the 
UPA Government, interest rate during the years 2003-04,2004-05 was 9.5 per cent. Now, h is 
8.5 per cent. Although the interest rate has come down, on behalf of the union, we are trying 
to do our best in this direction and the matter is under consideration of the Government. That 
is the difference between the NDA and UPA. 
Sir, now I come to other important issues that have  been mentioned by Mr. Raja and 
Mr. Sanjeeva Reddy. I do not want to repeat these p oints but I would like to mention about 
the policy with regard to the contract labour worki ng in the Central/State Government or its 
Corporation. Sir, the number of these workers is ve ry high. Sir, many people demand that 
the contract labour should get equal wage and that the contract labour should be 
regularized. But, Sir, for the information of the H ouse, I would like to mention that in this 
regard, the Hon'ble Supreme Court has given decisions in Airports Authority case of Bombay 
and Electricity case of Gujarat, wherein it said that the contract labour should be regularized, 
and, the contract labour was regularized. But, now, again the Hon'ble Supreme Court gave 
a decision that the contract labour, even though they had worked, could not be regularized. 
There has been another ruling wherein the Hon'ble Court remarked, even though they have 
been doing the same work, they cannot claim the same wages as they have not been recruited 
under the same procedure of recruitment. 
My submission to the hon. Minister—I am not saying anything against the Court—is to

consider bringing out a special legislation to give  them benefits in view of the Supreme 
Court's judgment. 
Sir, another decision is there. The Supreme Court, in one case, says that the appropriate 
Government is the administrative department. That has also created complication because 
the Central Government does not have the infrastructure to implement all the actual rules. It 
is only the State Governments which are implementing the rules and Acts in the respective 
States. So, when you say the administrative department is the appropriate Government, then, 
in case of the Industrial disputes Act or the Centr al Contract Labour Act, it automatically 
requires authorization of the Central Government to take up this matter. So, I think, it is also 
needed and the Indian Labour Conference and the Sta nding Committee also earlier 
recommended to amend this Act and say that the appropriate Government means the State 
Government or the Central Government and not the administrative Government. 
Sir, in this case, I want to mention one more thing also. The Government has constituted 
a new Wage Board for the working journalist and other non-journalist newspaper employees. A 
committee has been constituted. I do not know some people say that members have not 
been nominated and the time-frame is 3 years. Why i s it so? I think, the hon. Minister can 
give some information about the Wage Board of the journalists. I would like to know whether the 
Government is also trying to develop a machinery for the finalization of the electronic media 
journalists who are working there. 
The next point is, there are journalists all over the country. We know that the journalists in 
the country are in millions, having identity cards,  but no minimum wages. There are no 
minimum wages in the regional newspapers. There are also journalists who are given identity 
cards and asked to do their work. That is the fourth pillar of this country whom we believe in 
and to whom we are giving the facilities. Are we giving facilities to the newspaper owner or to 
the journalist? So, if the journalist is not getting the minimum wages, how can he function? It is 
also required to see that all the journalists who are working around the country, they should 
get not only the identity cards, but they should also get the minimum wages, at least, in the 
regional language newspapers. Aslo, I do not find many people really giving the Wage Board 
which has been awarded.

Castes, labour belonging to the Scheduled Tribes, labour belonging to the OBC, labour belonging to 
woman, who virtually is an outcaste in many ways, and labour belonging to child, they are all badly off. 
We have just to look into it, and we have to face the truth, and I think, Sir, we all will realise that there is 
something wrong somewhere which needs to be corrected. What are the steps to be taken? This 
is to be ' looked into by those who are at the helm of affairs. Skilled labour is there, unskilled labour 
is there, semi-skilled labour is there. The effort should be that unskilled labour becomes semi-skilled 
through training, semi-skilled becomes skilled through training. That process has to be done. That is 
conspicuous by its absence. One more factor to which I would like to draw the attention of the House 
is this. Many points have been already beautifully spelt out, and a maiden speech was also remarkable. 
For the first time, I have listened during the last so many years such an eloquent and such a factual, 
statistics-oriented and logical maiden speech for which is pay my salutation to Shri Rangarajan. 
Another maiden speech was also of a very good calibre. Anyhow, I would like to draw the attention 

222    Government [RAJYA SABHA]  Bill  
of the hon. Minister regarding diseases created by employment hazards-which have not 
been talked over. Hence, I am talking of that. Thos e who work in the carpet industry, they 
get asthama, it may be Badhoi or it may be Jaipur, or it may be any place. Those who work 
in the beedi indsutry in South India, they get nico tine poison, those who work in the glass 
industry at Ferozabad or elsewhere, little children , they get lead poisoning, those who 
work in mica mines, they get their lungs totally fi lled up with mica dust, those who work in 
hazardous fire crackers factory in Sivakasi or some where, which we enjoy on Diwali, they 
burn their own houses by that, and they burn their fingers daily, those who work in brick 
kilns and bajri ki khanc, they also suffer from one disease or the other. Wha t I wanted to 
draw attention was, the L abour Ministry should take care. It is already taking care, perhaps. 
But more care is required to be taken of diseases which are outcome of direct employment. 
Firstly, how to prevent them, and if they occur, th en to cure them is their responsibility. 
(Time Bell) I close, Sir, as you desire that way, and the time is also over. But I would like to say 
that social security is very important for labout. First is right to employment, which we have not 
granted so far. I will say all kudos for this UPA Government provided they grant two rights—
we will be with them right to employment, constitutional right, and right to strike to the labout. If 
that happens, I think it will go in annuls in golden words. Sir, there is a need for social security 
for labout, insurance, drinking water, food securit y, health security, education security, 
maternity security, disability security, old-age security etc. I think, our hon. Minister is so well 
read and so well oriented that he will take care of all of them, and I close it, Sir, by making out 
one point, hough out of context, that an impression  was created as if adverse reflection 
was being made on the hon. Minister for Labour; it is not at all there. We all say he is one of 
very competent, one of very able, one of very noble  persons, and what we all wanted to 
convey was, because of his ability, because of his erudition, because of his goodness, we 
wished and prayed and wanted, let this New Year bring him an elevation and let him be the 
Cabinet Minister so that the Ministry gets proper r ecognition that labour empowerment is 
very important! Otherwise, there was no disparagement. That is what I want to put on record. 
Thank you very much, sir. 
SHRI SANJAY RAUT: Sir, a number of times, this augu st House has discussed the 
problems faced by the country's labour force, and the action being taken by the Government 
to improve their lot. Today, I want to bring to the notice of the Government, through you, Sir, 
some basic problems being faced by the labour, and the difficulties being faced in their 
welfare. 
Sir, the most important problem is the numerous lab our laws passed by the Parliament 
during the last six decades, which are being implemented by the State Governments. Sir, with 
the opening up of our economy, during the last 15-18 years, new problems have cropped up, 
which are not catered to by the present laws, leading to their exploitation. This has resulted 
in exploitation of labour, especially woman workers. There is no Minimum Wages Act for this 
sector, leading to the exploitation of workers. 
However, this is one aspect of our labour laws. Som e of the provisions of our existing 
laws have become chaotic and these need to be revie wed. I, therefore suggest that the 
Government should review all the labour laws, presently under force, and come out with a 
minimum number of Acts, making them comprehensive to cover the situations which have 
been thrown up by the liberalised economy. 
Sir, a large number of women workers are employed i n unorganised sectors. The 
problems'faced by woman workers are very serious. Woman workers are not paid equal to 

Government [23 APRIL, 2008] Bill   223 
their male counterparts, in spite of our constituti onal mandate of 'equal pay for equal 
work'. The woman workes face the problem of safety, and they are not treated with dignity 
by their male colleagues or superiors. 
Sir, multiplicity of laws has raised yet another pr oblem also. A large portion of our 
labour force is neo-literate or semi-literate, maki ng it difficult for them to apprehend and 
take benefits of these laws extended for them. To m y mind, NGOs, here, can play a very 
important role in making workers in unorganised sec tors fully aware of the laws. In fact, 
there is no effective protection available for the labour force working in unorganised 
sectors. There are no laws available to protect the m. "There is maximum exploitation in 
this sector. 
Sir, the exploitation of labour is not restricted t o unorganised sectors alone, but it is 
there in the organised sector also. Beedi manufactu ring sector is one of the sectors in our 
country which employs a sizeable number of workers in State like Maharashtra, Madhya 
Pradesh, Andhra Pradesh, karnataka, Bihar, Jharkhan d and Tamil Nadu. Due to their 
occupation they are often exposed to T.B. and other  chronic diseases. But no proper 
medical facilities such as medical health centre ar e being made available to them for their 
health care. 
There is a Housing Scheme for beedi workers. The progress of the Scheme is very slow 
and needs to be accelerated. Most of the workers ar e not aware of this Scheme and are 
unable to take benefits because of their lack of aw areness. Workers are unable to claim a 
good number of benefits available to them under various schemes and labour laws. Now, I 
suggest that the Government should take immediate steps to launch an awareness campaign. 
Sir, there is a big problem of child labour, which the Government needs to pursue vigorously. 
About 1.5 crore children have been identified in 58  hazardous areas. This is a problem 
connected with the socio-economic conditions of the  families. The main reason for child 
labour in the country is poverty. 
Sir, the Government is implementing a Scheme called "National Child Labour Project." It is 
being implemented in 300 districts. But its implementation leaves much to be desired. I would 
like to draw the attention of this august House to the condition of child labour in the 
metropolitan city of Mumbai. There are many cases of child labour and, unfortunately, most 
of these children come from backward States. 
Sir, Maharashtra is one of the most advanced States in industrial activity. The number of 
workers employed in the organised sector in Maharas htra is, perhaps, the highest in the 
country. However, thousands of industries, small an d big, are now closed. In the last five 
years, more then 15,000 small scale industries are closed and more then 84,000 industrial 
workers are out of job. Similarly, during the same period more than 900 medium and big 
industries are closed and more then 1,40,000 industrial workers have lost jobs in Maharashtra 
State alone. The condition of these jobless workers is very precarious. 
Sir, there are complaints that most of the industrial units are not depositing the legal share 
of the workers towards the Provident Fund. It need to be looked into thoroughly. It should 
now be ensured that the legal share of the workers is deposited by the employers in the 
Provident Fund so that in time of need the workers could get their due share. 

224   Government [RAJYA SABHA] Bill  
Sir, a major area of concern is the enforcement of various laws relating to labour welfare. 
THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (PROF. P.J. KURIEN): Sanjayji, please conclude. 
SHRI SANJAY RAUT: Sir, I would take one more minute only. Though this part is mainly the 
concern of the State Governments, there is lack of efforts in the strict implementation of 
these laws. There are Labour Tribunals, both Centra l and State, where a large number of 
cases are pending for a number of years. Through you Sir, I request the Government to give 
a serious thought to these problems which are affecting our labour sector. 
Sir, with these words, I conclude and thank you.

THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (PROF. P.J. KURIEN): Thank you. Now, the hon. Minister.  
SHRITAPAN KUMAR SEN (West Bengal): Sir, I also want  to speak on this.  
THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (PROF. P.J. KURIEN): Yes, you jus t take two minutes.  
SHRI TAPAN KUMAR SEN: Sir, through you, I would jus t like to draw the attention of the House to 
the whole allocation pattern of this Labour Budget which has demonstrated a total disrespect to the 
unanimous conclusion of the 40th Indian Labour Conf erence, which concluded, after a thorough review 
of the implementation status of the labour laws thr oughout th^ country, both in the organised and in 
unorganised sectors, that the labour enforcement ma chineries to be modernised, to be strengthened 
with additional strength by augmenting the total st rength, which includes the CGITS, which includes 
both the administrative and the judicial enforcemen t machinery. So, your expenditure pattern has 
shown a total disrespect to a unanimous conclusion of a tripartite forum. This is really condemnable.  
So, the second point is that when the Indian Labour  Conference has expressed concern over the 
tragic status of the implementation of the labour l aws and when that was stressed upon, thereafter 
the Government action, the only legislative action that has been taken to allow more liberty to the 
employers to violate labour laws legally by introducing a Bill which allow i establishments employing up 
to 40 persons not to submit any return, they are fr ee from all obligations to submit any return, there by 
they freely violate the labour laws. The same patte rn was folloWed thereafter in the ESI by allowing 
self-certification in the matter  

Governmeni (23 APRIL, 2008] Bill   227  
of ESI implementation in all establishments employing up to 40 employees. That means, in 
more than 60 per cent of the industrial workforce in the organised sector itself, I am not speaking 
about the unorganised sector at all, you are legitmising labour law violation. That is why my 
colleague has rightly described that in this era you are promoting labour law violations, and your 
Budget bears the stamp of that. My last point, agai n, a unanimous recommendation of the 
Standing Committee on Labour on the Unorganised Sec tor Bill — it was a unanimous 
recommendation — (Time-bell) I am concluding. But it is unfortunate that two days back from the 
Ministiry an official amendment to the Unorganised Labour Social Security Bill was circulated and 
by that it is clearly understood that the unanimous recommendation cutting across party lines to 
improve upon the Bill has been totally ignored. (Time-bell) If a Parliamentary forum's unanimous 
recommendation is disrespected and ignored in this fashion, I think, that is a very bad situation. 
(Time-bell) I am just concluding. It is dejection of the entire House cutting across party lines. 
Right from the Treasury Benches to the Opposition B enches they have expressed their 
dejection and the dejection is (Time-bell) in this kind of disrespect to labour who created value 
for the society and who are allowing the Government to boast of 8.9 per cent GDP growth. 
(Time-bell) They are the creators of this value. (Time-bell) They do not deserve this kind of 
disrespect. I urge upon the Labour Minister to please correct this. Thank you.

I salute the workers for the contribution they have made in building this naton. Sir, I would like to 
place my point of view first before you and the House and then I will reply to the points raised by the 
hon. Members. While making my points I would be covering some of the major points raised by our 
Members. I would also thank D. Rajaji for initating the debate and also the new Members who have 
made very, very valuable contribution, maybe, for the first time, they have spoken in this House, 
but they have spoken as veterans with a lot of experience they have in the field of labour.The 
mandate of my Ministry is to protect and safeguard the interests of the workers in general and those 
who constitute the poor, deprived and working sections of the society in particular with due regard 
for creating a healthy work environment, higher production and productivity to develop and coordinate 
vocational, skill training and employment services to promote welfare and provide social security 
to the labour force both in the organised and unorganized sectors and maintain a harmonious 
relations/solutions all in tandem with the process of economic and social development. Sir, for me to 
carry on my work, I must go on record to thank the Prime Minister Dr. Manmohan Singh who has given 
us all the guidance and also Shrimati Sonia Gandhi, the UPA Chairperson, for making this a major point in 
our UPA Common Minimum Programme which is the guideline for us to take it forward. Maybe there 
have been criticisms saying that we are not following the UPA guidelines. But, I would like to say, 
whatever retrograde steps were taken, we have set right in this Parliament so that the workers will 
get their due and I  asure the House 

228    Government [RAJYA SABHA] Bill  
nothing will be done to disturb the harmony between the management and the workers. The 
workers will get their right. The Government will stand up and fight for the workers. Many a 
times, when negotiations have taken place, many a times when discussions have taken place 
with my officers, I have always said, I may be a Mi nister but when the question of workers 
come I will be a sitting on the side of the workers'. So, I assure the House that I will be with the 
workers to fight for their rights. The points relat ing to the Ministry of Labour and 
Employment in the National Common Minimum Programme — which was raised by Rajaji— are 
programmes relating to the enhancement of the welfare and well-being of the farmers, farm 
labour and the workers, particularly, those in the unogranised sector and assure to secure 
future for their families in every respect, ensurin g the fullest implementation of the 
Common'Minimum Programme, Wage Laws to farm labour and enactment of 
comperehensive protective legislation for all agric ultural workers striving for elimination of 
child labour, re-examination of the labour laws, to  reduce Inspector Raj and consultation, 
consensus and cooperation to strengthen labour mana gement relations. We have taken 
action to achive the objectives, some of which I sh all be describing in detail. The vision of 
Ministry of Labour and Employment is to provide soc ial protection to unorganised sector 
workers, eliminate child labour by adopting the seq uential approach starting with the 
hazardous sector, enlarge the coverage of vocationa l training and enhance its quality to 
reach world standards. A lot of concern was express ed about the ITIs and the standards. 
Rajaji, you had raised these issues. Vocational tra ining enhances its quality to reach world 
standards, generate awareness among workers regarding their legal and welfare entitlements, 
promote occupational safety and health measures. Th ere was a concern expressed about 
the workers' health. I have taken it up with the ES IC and said that it is not that we provide 
treatment to a worker when he goes to a hospital but we should have annual check up of all 
the workers coming under ESIC so that preventive tr eatment could be given and we have 
allotted extra money for this particular purpose. T here was a mention to promote 
occupational safety and health measure, maintain ha rmonious industrial relation situation, 
compile consumer index numbers for industrial worke rs and revise the base from time to 
time, increase the social security reach of the Employees Provident Fund Organisation and 
Employees' State Insurance Corporation for organise d sector workers. Out entire intention 
is to bring all the organised sectors under the pro vident fund and the ESI Corporation so 
that both the workers will get social security, pro mote international cooperation in labour 
matters and amend the labour legislations to bring them in tune with the changing needs. 
For this purpose, we receive both Plan and Non-Plan  funds. On the Plan side, during 2007-
08, the first year of the Eleventh Plan, the Ministry initially allocated only Rs. 345 crores. This 
included the civil work component of Rs. 19.52 cror es. This was increased substantially to 
Rs. 1250 crores at the Revised Estimates stage. Since the Ministry of Finance allowed us for 
further re-appropriation, our Plan expenditure duri ng 2007-08 was about Rs. 1275 crores. 
This was approximately 392 per cent of the Budget E stimate and 102 per cent of the 
Revised Estimates and 566 per cent over expenditure  of year 2006-07. Shri Raja has 
expressed his concern about it. For the year 2008-0 9, our Plan allocation is Rs. 800 crores 
including Rs. 28.50 crores for civil works component. This may further increased at the R.E. 
stage as we expect to sustain the present type of activities and expenditure. Shri Tapanji has 
also raised a very important issues. I think, we wi ll also provide necessary funds to extend 
the benefit to the workers. 
The Non-Plan allocation for the Ministry for 2007-0 8 was Rs. 1571.79 crores and for 
2008-09 is Rs. 1721.57 crores respectively. The actual expenditure was Rs. 1638.64 crores

which is 95.18 per cent. That means, we reached a l evel of 95 per cent utilisation in the 
Ministry. I am sure, with our continued diligence, we will be able to achieve more effective 
target-expenditure in future. 
Sir, there are three areas which are of immense importance to us. As you are aware, for 
providing social security masures to the unorganise d sector workers, as mandated in the 
NCMP, a new Bill, namely, the Unorganised Sector Workers Social Security Bill, 2007, was 
introduced in this House. Many hon. members have ra ised about the issue of the 
recommendations of the Standing Committee. I assure the House, in our Bill, we have taken 
care of all the points raised in the Standing Committe, except creation of fund. The view of the 
Government is whatever money is required will be pr ovided. It is not that we are only 
covering the unorganised sector workers in this i.e ., people who are living Below Povery 
Line. What we have done now is, to cover the people  from the Below Poverty Line under 
various schemes. I am going to explain three scheme s. Sir,even people from the Above 
Poverty Line will also be covered to get social sec urity. It provides for formulating suitable 
welfare schemes on matters relating to life and disability cover, health and maternity benefit, 
old age protection and any other benefit as may be determined by the Central Government. 
Simultaneously, a health insurance scheme — Rashtri ya Swasthya Bima Yojana — for poor 
was launched on 1st October, 2007, by releasing the guidelines. Under this scheme, all the 
Below Poverty Line families will be covered in the next five years. That means, six crore 
families which comes to 30 crore people will be covered under the Scheme whereby we will be 
providing Rs. 30,000 to each family which is not a small measure. I think the House should 
appreciate the initiative taken by the Government. 
SHRI TAPAN KUMAR SEN: It is not meant for unorganis ed sector workers. It is for the 
workers who are from the Below Poverty Line. Given the definition of your parameters and 
the way you are deciding a BPL family, there is a c ontradiction between the Planning 
Commission and your Ministry ....(Interruptions)...  
SHRI OSCAR FERNANDES: We will take up that issue. T he Central Government will 
contribute 75 per cent of the premium. The Scheme envisages issue of a smart card to the 
beneficiary. This card will facilitate cashless transaction up to Rs. 30,000 so that the worker 
does not have to pay anything to seek medical treatment. The Scheme will be implemented 
in a phased manner to cover 1.2 crore BPL family workers in the first and all the six crore BPL 
workers will be covered by the end of 2012-13. This scheme has started becoming operational 
from 1st April, 2008. Fifteen States have advertised for seeking support from the insurance 
companies to roll out the scheme in their respective Statges. The smart cards' started rolling in 
the States of Rajasthan and Haryana during March, 2008, and in Delhi during April, 2008. We 
are concerned about various categories of unorganis ed sector workers. Apart from the 
unorganised security workers' Social Security Bill,  which has already been introduced in 
Parliament, and the three schemes, namely the Rashtriya Swasthya Beema Yojana, the Aam 
Aadml Beema Yojana and the Old Age Pension Scheme. We are examining the possibility of 
evolving social security schemes for segments of wo rkers one-by-one. To begin with, we  
trying to seek that the social security cover could be provided . 3 safai karamcharis, domestic 
workers, cycle-rickshaw pullers, and others. We are  also exam;'., g the possibility of 
extending the Rashtriya Swasthya Beema Yojana to other unorganised sector workers 
who are above the poverty line. This is the point I would like to emphasise upon. 
Secondly, in pursuance of the Government's commitme nt to eliminate child labour in 
hazardous areas, the National Child Labour Project (NCLC) Scheme has been extended to

cover 250 districts. Our future approach will be to  identify districts where chronically child 
labour is there, and attack that problem in those d istricts that are sending the highest 
number of children for child labour. And, not onl!y deal with the children, we would like to deal with 
the families by identifying the family from where the child has come and see that all the poverty 
alleviation programmes benefit that family so that the child is not sent for child labor. This we 
have, in the Ministry, has already initiated. An ho n. Member had raised this issue that we 
should try to identify such families. We have alrea dy taken action to go back to the family 
and see their conditions. A major activity undertaken under the National Child Labour Project 
Scheme is to establish a special school to provide non-formal education, vocational training, 
supplementary nutrition, stipend, health and care, etc. to children withdrawn from 
employment. About three 3.94 lakh children from spe cial schools of the National Child 
Labour Projects have been mainstreamed into the for mal education system. In addition, a 
40 million US dollar project on child labour has al so been launched in 21 districts. The 
additional features of this scheme includes vocatio nal training to adolescents and 
strengthening public education, in coordination wit h Education Department, monitoring and 
tracking of child labour and provide viable income generation alternatives to their families, 
etc. Employment of children working as domestic ser vants and working in teashops and 
dhabas, etc. has been prohibited under the Child Labour Pro hibition Act, 1986, w.e.f. 10th 
October, 2006. A campaign has been launched for cre ating public awareness through 
media, and for sensitising the concerned officials and stakeholders through meetings, 
workshops and discussions. A nation-wide enforcement and awareness drive was launched 
for a fortnight on the occasion of Children's Day. As poverty is the primary cause of child 
labour, educational rehabilitation of such children  is complemented by economic 
rehabilitation of the families of the child labour through convergence approach by covering 
them under the benefits of the various Ministries a nd Departments. We intend to involve 
fully the institution of Panchayati Raj. We intend to take the services of the schools and 
also the Panchayats. We will request all the Pancha yats to see that no child is left without 
schooling facility. This will be monitored by the P anchayats. We will be requesting the 
Panchayati Raj Ministry to help us in this effort. The teachers will be asked to tell us if there 
are any drop-outs, so that we can go after that family and see that that child is brought back 
to school. This will be our approach to deal with t he child labour problem. Thus, they will be 
the active partners and stakeholders in our effort to eliminate child labour. 
Thirdly, vocational training, with a view to creati ng a world-class skilled labour force, is 
being given maximum importance. Mr. Raja, you were asking us where we have reached. 
You wanted to know whether it was only an assurance  given by the hon. Finance Minister 
or whether we were just trying to change the name o f the scheme. No, we are almost 
implementing the first programme initiated and anno unced by the Finance Minister. The 
hon. Prime Minister announced a 'Mission' programme. It is a bigger programme. Both are 
going on. 
We have the advantage of having a predominantly you ng population vis-a-vis the 
rest of the world. There will be increasing opportunities of work being outsourced to India as 
well as for our workforce to the world abroad, if we are able to retain our competitive edge. 
Training courses are offered through a network of a bout 5,465 Industrial Training Institutes 
and Industrial Training Centres located all over the country. About 0.75 million training seats 
are available at the Industrial Training Institutes ; with reservation for women, about whom 
we have expressed concern, the Scheduled Castes, th e Scheduled Tribes, disabled, ex-
servicemen, etc. 

Government [23 APRIL, 2008] Bill   231 
As announced by the Union Finance Minister in his B udget Speech 2004-05, action has 
been initiated for upgrading 100 Industrial Trainin g Institutes from domestic resources and 
400 Industrial Training Institutes through the World Bank assistance as Centres of Excellence 
for producing multi-skilled workforce of world standard. In his Budget Speech of 2007-08, the 
hon. Finance Minister announced that .1,396 Industrial Training Institutes would be upgraded 
into Centres of Excellence in specific trade skills  under the public-private partnership. The 
modalities of implementing the announcement are being worked out in consultation with the 
State Governments. Steps have been taken to upgrade , at least, 300 Industrial Training 
Institutes every year, beginning 2007-08. 
It has been decided by the Ministry of Labour and E mployment to commemorate the 
60th Anniversary of the Factories Act, 1948 by obse rving the year 2008 as the year of 
industrial safety and health. We are more concerned  about the workers health and safety. 
To make a beginning, one day national seminar or the theme, 'Industrial Safety and Health' 
- Vision 2020; Challenges and Strategies' is scheduled to be held at the SCOPE Convention 
Centre, Scope Complex, New Delhi on 28.4.2008. It w ill inculcate the culture of safe 
production and sustainable growth. 
I may add that the Parliamentary Standing Committee  on Labour deliberates on the 
Demands for Grants of the Ministry as well as other  important labour-related issues and 
makes important recommendations which we try to imp lement earnestly and keep both the 
Houses informed about the actions taken. Similarly,  we also take into account the 
recommendations of the National Commission on Labou r while bringing about changes in 
various labour laws. For example, in the Bonus Act, the Commission recommended Rs.7,500 
as the ceiling, but we went beyond that and raised it to Rs. 10,000. We are also trying to 
ensure that the contract workers receive their legi timate benefits. On the contract labour, 
there is a demand that the people who have served, at least, for ten years should be regularised. 
We have taken up this issue in the tripartite meetings. We have also taken up the issue with 
the managements and we are trying to impress on the m that they should come to some 
settlement on this issue. During the last year, a number of amendments were carried out in the 
central labour laws. The payment of Bonus Act, 1965, which provides for payment of bonus to 
employees of factories and establishments employing 20 or more persons has been amended to 
enhance the eligibility limit from Rs.3,500/-, to R s. 20,000/- and calculation ceiling from 
Rs.2,500/- to Rs.3,500/- per month while making emp loyees employed through contractors 
on building operations eligible for payment of bonu s under the Act. For the first time, 
contract workers in the unorganised sector have bee n brought under the purview of the 
Bonus Act. The amendments came into force w.e.f. 1.4.06. The Apprentice Act, 1961, has also 
been amended inter alia providing for reservation for backward classes. The  Bill to amend 
the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 to enhance medical bonus from Rs.250/- to Rs. 1,000/- was 
passed in both the Houses of Parliament. Here, we could not discuss it, but a suggestion has 
been made in the Lok Sabha that we should raise it beyond Rs. 1,000, that we had planned. 
The Government is empowered to enhance it. We will be considering it and, maybe, instead 
of Rs. 1,000 we will raise it to Rs.2,000/-, and pe riodically, we have the powers to enhance 
it, There is a provision to raise it up to Rs.20,00 0/-. Every three years it will be reviewed. 
Besides, a number of legislative proposals, such as  Unorganised Sector Workers' Social 
Security Bill, as mentioned by me earlier, the Bill to amend the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972, to 
cover the teachers in educational institutions whic h is a very important thing, — we 
received a lot of representations on this — the Bil l to amend the labour laws (Exemption 
from Furnishing Returns and Maintaining Registers by certain Establishments) Act, 1988, 

232   Government [RAJYA SABHA] Bill  
— here, we have to have further consultations and w e will be doing that — the Bill to 
amend section 66 ol'the Factories Act, 1948, so as to provide flexibility in matters of 
employment of women during night shift with adequat e safeguards for their safety, dignity, 
honour and transportation from factory premises to the nearest point of their residence are 
pending consideration, either in Lok Sabha or Rajya  Sabha. I may also state that the 
proposals to amend the (a) the Employees State Insu rance Act, 1948, to enable utilisation 
of medical facilities of the Employees' State Insur ance Corporation for implementing the 
Rashtriya Swasthya I3ima Yojana, (b) to amend the E mployment Exchange (Compulsory 
Notification of Vacancies) Act, 1959, to change the nomenclature of Employment Exchange to 
Employment Guidance and Promotion Centres to give primacy to employment, 
promotion, vocational guidance and counselling.........(c) to amend the Industrial Disputes 
Act, 1947 in respect of grievances redressal author ity, relaxation of qualifications of 
Presiding Officers, power to enforce decree by trib unals — this is one major suggestion 
that has come about — direct reference of dispute, etc., and (d) to amend the Plantation 
Labour Act, 1951 to change the definition of the em ployer, family and worker, adding a 
new chapter on safety bringing it in line with the provisions of the Child Labour (Prohibition & 
Regulation) Act, 1986 are at different stages of co nsideration. With the goodwill of both 
Houses, Sir, our efforts in this regard will achieve fruition. 
Sir, we have taken various other important initiati ves. We have referred the demand of 
the employees for grant of interim rates of wages t o working journalist — this point was 
raised in the House — and non-journalist newspaper employees to the Wage Boards for 
their examination and making suitable recommendatio ns. They want interim relief. This 
matter is being considered by the Wage Board. We have referred it to the Wage Board. We 
also propose to fix the minimum wages for the first  time in respect of "Employment of 
Sweeping and Cleaning excluding activities prohibit ed under the Employment of Manual 
Scavengers and Construction of Dry Latrines (Prohib ition) Act, 1993," etc. Here, Sir, the 
point I would like to make is, many of our workers are treated as contract workers. At 
times, they are not even given minimum wages, so, through this legislation, we are trying to 
fix the wages to such a level that they may draw, at least, if not equal to the wages that the 
class IV employees get but very near to the wages of the Class IV employees so that will be 
a deterrent for the people not to engage people under this. 
Sir, my Parliamentary Affairs Minister is saying that I have taken enough time.
